replicates both object points and relative poses in a 3D space using neural networks.
We achieve optimal performance in challenging pose-inference tasks, outperforming
state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. NDFs enable effortless transfer
to new objects without the need for retraining, as we demonstrate in experiments
involving manipulation tasks with unknown objects. Furthermore, NDFs can determine
whether two objects are identical simply by comparing their descriptor fields without
requiring prior knowledge. We show that NDFs are robust to varying viewing angles
and can be trained using a relatively small dataset. With NDFs, we successfully
trained a robot to pick up novel objects from a dataset of 13 known objects.

This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl curvature tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, this derivation serves as an introductory step for exploring more advanced topics in General Relativity, including the complex coefficient calculations for the Ricci tensor, the scalar curvature, and the Einstein field equations. By utilizing these complex coefficients, we obtain specific solutions to Einstein's field equations, represented in the Weyl curvature matrix framework. This review also outlines the procedure for converting these complex coefficients back to the original Minkowski space basis, thereby recovering the original form of the electromagnetic field. Additionally, we provide appendices detailing the derivation steps, the relationship between the complex null tetrad basis and the Minkowski space basis, as well as the Weyl curvature matrix and its eigenvalues. Identifying appropriate models for biological networks, specifically polymer systems, is a complex task due in part to the large amount of available data and intricate nature of these networks. I propose a 3-step method for model fitting: first, a linear regression technique is used to create a preliminary model, next the model is refined through the application of non-negative least squares, and finally this model is used as the basis for an integer programming problem to constrain and validate the results. This technique is demonstrated using a synthetic dataset and real-world Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum sensing data. The resulting models can be analytically interpreted to some extent, however, this technique is primarily useful for predicting unknown conditions. In addition, I discuss some issues with previous analyses of the Pseudomonas aeruginosa data. Code-mixed NLP deals with text that combines two or more languages, reflecting the linguistic patterns of bilingual or multilingual communication. While primarily observed in social media, online content also exhibits code-mixing in multiple language pairs, presenting code-mixed NLP challenges across various tasks including sentiment analysis, information extraction, and machine translation. To tackle real-world applications, research aims to develop high-performance models that effectively handle code-mixed data, though current code-mixed datasets fall short of fully utilizing all available linguistic resources, with many employing limited labels and lacking gold standards for evaluation. Furthermore, existing models struggle to generalize beyond the language pairs used in training, and there's a need to explore preprocessing techniques to enhance model efficiency. By addressing these concerns, code-mixed NLP has the potential to benefit heavily multilingual languages pairs by leveraging previously unused resources. In this paper, we outline research opportunities in code-mixed NLP for Hindi-English, citing relevant studies and data preparation challenges. Moreover, we present a simple preprocessing technique, lemmatization, which enhances model performance, according to our findings. The proliferation of image description generators over recent years is attributable to the growing necessity to provide access to visually impaired individuals to visual content. Despite the progress made in this field, the task remains challenging due to the vast diversity of possible descriptions for the same image. In response, reference-based assessment methods have emerged as a way to evaluate the effectiveness of image description systems, using human-provided descriptions as a gold standard. In this work, we delve into the world of reference-based assessment, outlining the various approaches that have been developed to date. Furthermore, we outline some potential limitations of these methods, including the difficulty of accounting for the ambiguity inherent in language when evaluating the accuracy of generated descriptions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach, leveraging the structural aspects of descriptions to enhance their semantic meaning, and thus providing a more precise method of evaluating the similarity between human-provided and automatically generated descriptions. This proposed technique is demonstrated through a working example, in addition to its application in a real-world scenario, utilizing a crowd-sourced dataset of image descriptions. This dataset, known as the Reference Assessment Dataset, is made available to the research community for the first time. This research is further supplemented by a related survey on the evaluation methods for image description systems. This work is concluded by outlining some potential avenues for future research, including the integration of world knowledge into description assessments, as well as the development of more sophisticated methods for modeling the semantic meaning of descriptions. This research investigates the significance of a societal phenomenon known as "The Big Sort" in the dissemination of misinformation on Reddit. Based on theoretical insights from politics, sociology, and information diffusion, as well as empirical analysis of Reddit data and election results, our study reveals that demographic isolation, as seen in "The Big Sort," contributes to the spread of misinformation by exacerbating cognitive biases and limiting access to opposing views. We demonstrate that areas with high levels of sorting experience greater misinformation diffusion, and this effect is intensified during high-stress events like elections. Furthermore, our research shows that areas with low sorting scores have lower incidence rates of all types of misinformation and that this effect is more pronounced for politically engaged users. We also explore the financial, educational, and age components of sorting and show that demographic isolation due to these factors contributes to the spread of misinformation. Finally, our analysis suggests that measures that reduce cognitive biases and increase exposure to opposing views, such as electoral competition and media consumption, can mitigate the negative effects of "The Big Sort" on misinformation diffusion. This study's findings contribute to our understanding of the complex factors influencing the dissemination of misinformation and provides actionable insights for designing effective misinformation-reduction strategies. We propose further research into the causes and consequences of "The Big Sort" and the dynamics of misinformation diffusion on social media platforms like Reddit. We also outline potential policy and intervention-based solutions to address the issues surrounding "The Big Sort" and misinformation dissemination. Last but not least, we provide a concise overview of this research and its implications in an executive summary. Specifically, we leverage acoustic signal processing techniques and machine learning effectively to model the audio signals emitted when interacting with a particular system, and our approach enables the robotic system to hear the audio signals produced during interaction and use them to infer the state of its own gripper. The escalating utilization of magnetic resonance imaging in neuroscience research and clinical applications is prompting hospitals to rush into acquiring their own MRI machines, without adequate training or maintenance, which leads to poor image quality. This paper discusses a dataset that is currently available for developing and evaluating novel quality assurance methods, with a focus on generalizing to unseen machines, sites, and data modality modifications. This dataset comprises 20,000 3D brain MRI volumes from five centers, with corresponding quality scores and radiology reports. We also present an initial approach to addressing this multi-faceted generalization issue by using a patch-based quality assessment method in conjunction with report-based quality prediction. This technique leverages spatial information from low-quality patches to train a robust model, with a focus on site, site-machine, and site-matrix transfers. Our results show consistent performance across different centers, with a score of 0.83 for area under the curve indicating a relatively narrow performance dispersion among the centers. The study considers multiple key factors including: the structure of distribution networks, electric vehicle adoption rates, location-specific charging behaviors, charging station installations, and grid resilience. A robust optimization approach is presented to determine optimal infrastructure investments and operation policies that prioritize the recovery of distribution networks from disruptions. Using real-world data from Beijing, numerical experiments illustrate the potential benefits and drawbacks of investing in large-scale private electric vehicles to enhance distribution network resilience. Furthermore, comparisons are made between different charging infrastructure installations and various electric vehicle adoption scenarios, revealing that widespread private electric vehicle adoption can lead to increased infrastructure costs and reduced recovery costs for distribution networks. However, if recovery costs are given a higher weighting, investing in large-scale private electric vehicles can lead to enhanced distribution network resilience. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we explored the effects of lattice parameters on the electronic and magnetic properties of these materials. Lastly, our findings suggest that the AuCu3 structure is stable under equilibrium conditions, with no phase transitions to other structures in the calculated temperature range. Next steps could involve incorporating spin-orbit interaction and assessing the materials' thermal expansion and magnetic anisotropy. Lastly, we outline potential experiments, including neutron scattering and high-energy synchrotron radiation, to validate our results and facilitate further research.

Coxeter groups with the B2 property have a notable characteristic where any even element can be expressed as the product of two cycles with specific lengths. This feature has various implications, including in the study of alternating permutation characteristics. Furthermore, it provides the foundation for analyzing the behavior of the number of even elements within a particular cycle type. In fact, it can be an essential tool in examining the generalization of the B2 property from the context of finite classical groups. Specifically, it enables us to generalize the property of B2 in the context of the classical groups SL(n, F) for a given field F, provided that n exceeds the square root of half the size of the field F. In this paper, we also investigate the relationship between the B2 property and the existence of a specific subgroup within the group itself. Additionally, we introduce and examine the generalization of the B2 property in the context of the classical groups Sp(2n, F) for a given field F. Provided that n exceeds the square root of half the size of the field F, we find that the group Sp(2n, F) exhibits the B2 property when n equals 4. In this case, the property is inherited from a certain triply transitive subgroup generated by the group Sp(4, F) itself, subject to some minor adjustments for certain small field sizes. Moreover, we determine the structure of the 4-fold diagonal subgroups within the group Sp(4, F) for different field F, provided that n equals 4. By re-examining the Pantheon SN Ia dataset in combination with galaxy lensing candidates identified in the Hubble Source Catalog, we concentrated on lenses with a single SN Ia being lensed by one galaxy. It is crucial to focus on lenses with a single SN Ia being lensed by one galaxy in order to avoid over-counting the same gravitational lensing system multiple times. Assuming a uniform distribution of lenses and considering the limited field-of-view, we calculated the average number of such lenses affecting SN Ia observations within the Pantheon sample. Based on this analysis, we estimated a manageable 10% of SN Ia with detectable lensing effects, with a significant 2000 SN Ia showing some degree of lensing impact however slightly definable. Having established this, we went on to carry out a mock analysis on the remaining 90% of SN Ia with minimal lensing effects, utilizing a mock dataset created for us by researchers who simulated the behavior of SNe Ia and galaxy lensing within the Pantheon sample. We introduce a novel type of T-shaped optical junction, termed T hubs, 
with compact dimensions, specifically designed to couple two distinct Fano resonators in close proximity. Our T hubs are engineered to exhibit identical propagation modes in both photonic nanowires and a 2D silicon-on-insulator structure. This ensures that the light propagation characteristics are conserved when transferring from nanowires to the 2D SOI. Our study demonstrates that T hubs can be efficiently used to couple Fano resonators in both nanowire and 2D SOI configurations. In particular, we show that T hubs can be integrated into 2D SOI to create over-lapping light localisation areas with high sensitivity and large spectral width. Our findings also indicate that T hubs can be effectively employed to couple Fano resonators in nanowires, resulting in high refractive index sensitivity and large spectral width. Furthermore, we demonstrate that T hubs can be integrated into 2D SOI to create photonic structures with over-lapping light localisation areas, thus enabling the detection of small changes in the surrounding environment. Our proposed T hubs in the 2D SOI configuration exhibit refractive index sensitivities of up to 0.157 and 0.094 for the nanowire and 2D SOI configurations, with a corresponding shift in the central cavity of up to 0.5 microns. Our study also investigates the effects of misaligned T hubs on the light localisation areas within the Fano resonators, demonstrating that even with a 300 nm misalignment, the light localisation areas remain overlapping. This robustness to misalignment enables the T hubs to effectively couple Fano resonators in both nanowire and 2D SOI configurations. For a sequence of negatively correlated Bernoulli variables, we establish exponential decay of moment measures and a logarithmic decay of probability measures of large deviations. Additionally, we derive an estimate for the expected value of the negative part of a sum of such variables, with correlations measured using the total variation norm. We provide a novel approach to modifying symplectic transformations between subsets of a symplectic vector space, which we call symplectic alterations. Given two symplectic transformations u and v, an alteration from u to v for a specific vector is defined as the difference between the images of that vector under these transformations. We then seek the set of all alterations that form a closed vector space. Our results demonstrate that this particular vector space can be determined using specific properties of the transformation u, and it is closed under a particular operation. Furthermore, we provide concrete examples to illustrate this concept. Additionally, we establish a connection between these alterations and the derivatives of the Taylor series expansion of a particular function. This function, which can be derived from the alterations, has properties similar to the original function. This discovery also holds in the context of Riemannian geometry. Lastly, we explore the possibilities of extending these findings to more complex scenarios.

Transplant centers face a persistent issue where donated kidneys are rejected due to being incompatible with potential recipients. To address this challenge, we suggest introducing a new strategy, prioritizing kidneys based on their matching potential with multiple recipients. We have developed a theoretical framework to valuate this potential and calculate the ideal acceptance rate of incompatible kidneys. Our model indicates that accepting 20% of offered incompatible kidneys can result in a 14% increase in transplants, although this may vary depending on specific donation and recipient patterns. Additionally, our research reveals that incorporating kidneys based on their matching potential with a single recipient does not yield significant gains. To demonstrate the practical applications of this approach, we used real data from a transplantation center in the United States. Our analysis suggests that even without adjusting the current allocation rules, simply prioritizing kidneys based on their compatibility with a single recipient already results in a relatively high transplant rate. To maximize the benefits, however, it would be necessary to adjust the allocation rules to account for the compatibility of kidneys with multiple recipients, or implement alternative solutions such as paired kidney exchanges more extensively. Our research highlights the importance of interconnecting transplantation databases to facilitate exchanges and increase the utilization of donated kidneys. Our data further indicates that even a simple, non-ideal strategy of prioritizing kidneys based on their compatibility with a single recipient can lead to a notable increase in transplants, to the tune of 12% according to our analysis. Our research provides insights that can be used by transplantation centers and healthcare policymakers to improve the effectiveness of kidney transplants. Our data suggests that even a simple, non-ideal strategy of prioritizing kidneys based on their compatibility with a single recipient can lead to a notable increase in transplants, to the tune of 12% according to our analysis. Our research provides insights that can be used by transplantation centers and healthcare policymakers to improve the effectiveness of kidney transplants. Our findings have significant implications for the healthcare system, given that the number of people in need of kidney transplants far exceeds the available donations. Our research indicates that increasing ideal acceptance of incompatible kidneys could result in a 14% increase in transplants, to the tune of 840 transplants per year in the United States. Our analysis suggests that even without adjusting the current allocation rules, simply prioritizing kidneys based on their compatibility with a single recipient already results in a relatively high transplant rate. To maximize the benefits, however, it would be necessary to adjust the allocation rules to account for the compatibility of kidneys with multiple recipients, or implement alternative solutions such as paired kidney exchanges

Although widely adopted, we find issues with current evaluation metrics that overestimate the performance of models. To establish a clear baseline, we introduce two simple mathematical benchmarks to assess word representations. In addition to these benchmarks, we analyze the representation learning process and offer a generative model to mimic the representations learned. We also investigate the stability of the representations and find they vary significantly depending on the specific model used and the amount of data employed. Furthermore, we discover that the representations learned are similar to those obtained through other methods, without the need for the Loughran-McDonald technique. To demonstrate this, we include a practical application to Twitter sentiment classification. We find that the representations learned through this method are equivalent to those obtained using a classification model on sentiment-labeled data. In conclusion, representations learned using the Loughran-McDonald method simply categorize words as positive or negative, a task that other methods can accomplish without this specific technique. We believe this result has implications for the evaluation of pre-trained language models on polarity datasets. We make our code available online at https://github.com/wordhank/Polarity. This article presents single-input single-output orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (SISO-OFDM) and single-input single-output orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (MISO-OFDM) systems that serve as basic variants of our previously proposed Wideband Waveforming (WBW) architecture. By combining end-to-end optimization and the wideband information theory framework, we derive the optimal WBW parameters for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. Furthermore, through numerical evaluations, we demonstrate the performance benefits of these wideband solutions over their traditional counterparts in various scenarios. Additionally, by incorporating multiple-antenna technology, we find that MISO-OFDM often outperforms SISO-OFDM due to its increased scanning frequency. Lastly, we outline potential hardware implementations for these wideband systems, highlighting the simplicity of their OFDM-based structures.

These semi-discrete equations have been numerically solved using a Taylor-Galerkin finite element method. The results from these tests have been compared with the results obtained using the conservative level-set method, the embedded boundary method, and other numerical techniques. The results show that this new technique produces accurate and stable solutions for a range of problems, and these solutions compare favorably with the solutions obtained using other numerical techniques. The computational time required using this new technique has also been found to be less than the computational time required using the level-set method for some of the test cases. In multiagent competitions, having multiple equilibria can make it challenging to evaluate learning agents, especially when there's a desire to distinguish between "rational" and "irrational" behavior. We introduce a new metric, centered on a concept called the "rationalizable equilibrium," to address this issue. This metric identifies the unique equilibrium that maximizes the number of agents able to maintain a rational strategy in response to any possible opponent strategies. We develop two distinct methods for evaluating the rationalizable equilibrium in multiagent competitions and show that these approaches are applicable to a broad range of games, including those with multiple agents and uncertain payoff matrices. Furthermore, we contribute methods for acquiring the rationalizable equilibrium in online settings, including learning algorithms and procedures to accelerate learning in response to performance drops. Finally, our research encompasses an exploration of the relationship between the rationalizable equilibrium and other game theory-based metrics, offering insights into their respective sensitivities to the distribution of payoffs. We thoroughly evaluate our approaches and methods through comprehensive computational experiments and statistical analysis, comparing them to alternative methods and identifying key performance influencers. The resulting code is publicly available as an open-source repository. We also discuss the implications of our research for future competitions and evaluation protocols. The work described in this paper originated from the authors' efforts to design challenging environments for existing reinforcement learning agents. These environments, along with additional suggestions and insights, are presented in the appendix. We further propose the "rationalizable equilibrium" challenge as a potential problem of interest for the artificial intelligence community. The research described in this paper is relevant to a broad range of fields, including artificial intelligence, game theory, theoretical computer science, economics, statistics, and mathematics. This study examines how removing infected nodes from "small-world" networks during an epidemic outbreak affects the spread of a highly contagious virus. By modeling epidemics on networks that change structure as the epidemic progresses, we investigate how the introduction of a vaccination program that targets infected individuals reduces the spread of disease. Our results show that such a program accelerates an exponential growth phase but slows the epidemic's eventual decline. If the network is highly clustered, removing infected nodes can even lead to an apparent slowdown of the epidemic's early growth phase before ultimately accelerating its spread. As the efficacy of this vaccination program increases, we find that the basic reproduction number falls below 1 only after the exponential growth phase, and we explain this phenomenon by calculating an effective reproduction number. Our analysis also reveals that the epidemic decay becomes much slower as the vaccination program targets more random nodes. If the network has a scale-free component, the epidemic's behavior changes dramatically as the vaccination program targets infected nodes, as it shifts from an accelerated spread to a power law decline. Our analysis of these complex networks involves a simulation-estimated basic reproduction number, which we validate by comparing it to multiple expressions calculated analytically. Our findings are robust across various network and epidemic parameters and offer insights into how real networks respond to a vaccination program that targets infected individuals. If these networks resemble the models we studied, such a program may ultimately fail to control the spread of disease. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. This issue is particularly pronounced when dealing with proton-proton collision predictions, which can originate from multiple sources, including but not limited to, certain processes with identified hadrons, deep inelastic scattering off external fields, and some heavy flavor productions. To effectively combine these predictions, it is necessary to standardize their structure and component formats. This paper outlines a theoretical framework for collectively analyzing and fitting probability density functions, with a focus on incorporating collision data from particle detectors. To achieve this goal, we develop a comprehensive framework comprising two main components: (1) a set of rules governing the combination of predictions, (2) a numerical tool capable of automating this process. A distinguishing feature of this framework is its ability to combine not only data but also theoretical predictions on probability density functions, based on combined analyses of collision data from detectors. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, we present detailed examples, including but not limited to, processes with identified hadrons, heavy flavor productions, and semi-inclusive scattering off external fields. With this framework, we show that it is possible to reconcile Discrete Ordinacy Approximation and Monte Carlo methods through combined analyses of collision data from detectors. Furthermore, we illustrate the implications of incorporating scattering data off external fields on probability density functions, based on combined analyses of collision data from detectors. To facilitate widespread adoption, this framework is made available to the scientific community through a publicly accessible repository. Consequently, this framework can serve as a foundation for collectively analyzing and fitting probability density functions, with a particular emphasis on incorporating collision data from particle detectors. With its modular design, this framework can be applied to problems both related to but also beyond the scope of this paper. To facilitate further advancements, we outline potential extensions to this framework, including but not limited to, integrating additional collision production processes and heavy flavor productions with hadron colliders. With its focus on providing a comprehensive overview, this paper is directed towards but not limited to, researchers with a background in but not limited to, particle physics, hadron colliders, deep inelastic scattering, Monte Carlo methods, Discrete Ordinacy Approximation, and probability density functions. To improve policy enhancement methods, particularly reinforcement learning enhancements using experience replay, we propose a new exploration strategy that is designed to increase the variance of returns seen during exploration.  This new strategy, called Variance-Aware Experience Replay, first calculates the variance of returns for each state-action pair in the replay buffer.  It then prioritizes pairs with higher variances for selection in the policy enhancement process.  We hypothesize that increasing the variance of returns will accelerate policy enhancement by allowing the agent to simultaneously learn from both high-reward states and those with high uncertainty.  To validate this hypothesis, we tested Variance-Aware Experience Replay in the challenging Game of Drones and found that it significantly accelerates policy enhancement, even when compared to state-of-the-art methods.  We also analyzed the variance of returns in various contexts and found that it can be both a beneficial and detrimental factor for policy enhancement, depending on the specific game being played.  As a result, we propose a number of future research directions aimed at further exploring the relationship between variance of returns and policy enhancement. We introduce a method for conducting full N-body simulations in altered gravity theories with conformally coupled gravity at a rapid pace. This approach enables us to perform an extensive set of cosmological simulations in conformally coupled gravity across a range of scales and in multiple variants, thereby creating a comprehensive dataset for researchers. This achievement is made possible by leveraging the similarity between conformally coupled gravity and $\Lambda$CDM through a transformation, which allows us to repurpose existing $\Lambda$CDM N-body simulations with modified initial conditions to obtain conformally coupled simulations. We test and validate this method against N-body simulations conducted using a more straightforward approach and find it to be accurate for a broad range of cosmological scenarios. As a result, we create a comprehensive set of mock galaxy distributions in altered gravity theories that can be used for evaluating mock galaxy surveys and exploring the differences they exhibit when compared to $\Lambda$CDM. These simulations cover a wide range of scales and include simulations with biased systems, as well as those with unique initial conditions generated through the application of random field perturbations. These mock simulations are suitable for multiple galaxy formation models and can be used to compare the predicted galaxy distributions in conformally coupled gravity with observed galaxy datasets, thereby placing constraints on the parameters of this theory. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the ongoing exploration of altered gravity theories and provide valuable insights for the design of future galaxy simulations in conformally coupled gravity. These simulations are made available through the website of the Centre for Astrophysics and Supercomputing at the University of Melbourne. We invite researchers to visit this site and engage with the simulations in a variety of formats. The code used for these simulations is based on the RAMSES-Nbody N-body code and can be adapted for use with other codes. We discuss the scope for further improvements in this research, including the incorporation of galaxy formation models and the extension of these simulations to Hubble volumes. We also outline the potential applications of this research to other altered gravity theories and conformally coupled cosmological scenarios. The simulations conducted in this research are suitable for use with galaxy formation models and have been designed to match the scales of galaxy distributions in observed galaxy datasets. As such, they provide a precise match to observed galaxy datasets on large scales but exhibit deviations in small-scale regimes. We investigate the neutrino-induced decay of ultralight dark matter, specifically looking at how it could affect neutrinoless double beta decay and certain cosmological phenomena. Initially, we consider dark matter comprised of scalar or fermion 'photons' with a mass less than $10^{-13}$eV, which would allow neutrinos to interact with dark matter 'photons' due to their oscillations. This interaction could become significant when neutrinos encounter dark matter particles, either in the early universe or in the present day. We examine the implications for neutrinoless double beta decay and certain cosmological phenomena, such as the suppression of neutrino fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background and the overproduction of neutrinos in the early universe. If a non-zero value is observed for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude, it would necessitate a re-evaluation of the neutrino sector based on the decay's energy spectrum. Moreover, we discuss the relationship between this scenario and certain theoretical models, such as axion and scalar fields, and explore the potential for detection through experiments that involve neutrino or dark matter searches. Ultimately, we find that even when assuming a very long decay lifetime, the energy spectrum of the decay products exhibits a distinctive feature that could be exploited in future searches, and we identify a particular window of sensitivity for the future beta decay experiment nEXO-200. Additionally, we provide a straightforward method for incorporating dark matter interactions into neutrino oscillation equations and offer a preliminary estimate of the neutrino oscillation length characterizing this interaction. Lastly, we consider a variant of this scenario in which the interaction between neutrinos and dark matter occurs through a massive force carrier rather than directly, which would result in a significantly shorter neutrino oscillation length and make the energy spectrum's distinctive feature more challenging to detect, but we also identify a potential for detection in this variant. Nevertheless, this variant would likely remain undetected even with an increase in sensitivity in future experiments. Consequently, any detection of the distinctive energy spectrum's feature in beta decay experiments could be followed by searches for the effects of dark matter on neutrino oscillations, which would provide even more information about the neutrino sector. If the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude is found to be zero, it would allow for a lower bound on the dark matter particle mass, which could range from $10^{-14}$ to $10^{-12}$eV, and would also imply that the energy spectrum's distinctive feature is unlikely to be detected in beta decay experiments. By replacing the Bianchi identity with an over-determined system, we derive a generalized algebraic identity that leads to a specific nonlocal algebraic identity when combined with an appropriate integrability condition. This process results in the nonlocal gravity equations, which form a second-order differential system when combined with the Einstein equations. We also explore the implications of this approach for self-dual gravity and nonlocal Einstein gravity. Furthermore, we provide explicit solutions for nonlocal Einstein gravity in a flat background. Additionally, we introduce a nonlocal modification of the Einstein-Hilbert action in terms of tetrads and connection forms, which yields the same nonlocal gravity equations as the differential system derived from the Bianchi identity. This action can be expressed in terms of a nonlocal Fierz-Pauli-Lorentzian action integrated over the tetrads and connection forms, which is invariant under the Lorentz group. We also explore the linearized nonlocal gravity action in terms of the metric tensor and find that it corresponds to a nonlocal extension of the linearized Einstein theory with a specific nonlocal de Broglie-Bergson operator. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre indicate that many have remained inactive for extended periods, suggesting their outbursts may follow predictable patterns. By analyzing a sample of these sources, we found that their outburst intervals can deviate from regular cycles, and attributed this variability to the significant effects of general relativity on a specific class of binary systems. Specifically, sources with low-mass companions exhibit irregular outburst patterns due to the general relativistic effect of their outbursts interrupting the interaction between the neutron star and its companion, thus influencing the system's behaviour during quiescent periods. As a result, we expect sources with low-mass companions to exhibit shorter outburst periods than those with higher-mass companions. By considering these factors and modelling outburst patterns mathematically, we established a specific relationship between outburst periods and the masses of binary systems. Furthermore, we applied this understanding to the Galactic Centre sources and found that sources with low-mass companions would exhibit outburst periods in the range of a few to tens of years, and that many short-period sources may actually be active rather than quiescent, thus influencing the character of the Galactic Centre's variable X-ray sources. Consequently, we propose that the outburst periods of the Galactic Centre sources be monitored over longer periods in order to differentiate between sources with low and high mass companions, and to gain a more accurate understanding of the variable X-ray sources within the region. Lastly, we highlight the potential for general relativity to provide valuable insights into binary systems outside the Galactic Centre. The research described in this paper originated from the discussion section of Strader et al. (2012). The main contributions include deriving an explicit relationship between outburst periods and binary system parameters, as well as gaining insight into the variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre. The results can be validated by monitoring the outburst periods of the Galactic Centre sources over longer periods. users must navigate diverse meanings to achieve a common goal.  To mimic this 
challenge, we create a novel dataset, called Variety Inference Conversation, 
where each text pair in a conversation has multiple possible Sematic Inference 
relations.  To evaluate the diverse semantic relationships, a panel of native 
English speakers identifies nine categories of possible relations, including five 
INFERENCE types and four alternative varieties.  Our analysis shows that the 
most frequent relation is then defined as the primary inference standard, with 
which we assess pre-trained language models using Natural Language Inference data 
as a proxy.  To demonstrate variety's impact, we train models on both general 
NLI data and tailored Variety Inference Conversation data and compare their 
performance with the default BERT-based model.  Our results reveal that variety 
improves the model's performance when given diverse definitions but does not 
outperform the default model when given no variety.  To further explore variety 
in conversational dialogues, we collect a second dataset, Variety Dialogue 
Inference, where each text pair has multiple possible Sematic Inference relations 
and a statement that includes one of the possible relations.  Our analysis shows

evaluate the models, we use a scoring system based on the nine categories of

We present a comprehensive model for Gamma-Ray Burst afterglows, which incorporates the interplay of various processes that influence their development. The proposed framework takes into account the expansion of the cosmos, the movement of the burst source, the absorption of photons by electrons, and the emission of radiation. By integrating these factors, we derive an afterglow model that encompasses both relativistic and non-relativistic components. This model exhibits three distinct phases, separated by the time when the radiation becomes non-relativistic and when the observed afterglow starts to decline exponentially. By synthesizing extensive observational data, we establish that afterglow afterglows progress dynamically, influenced by the characteristics of their parent bursts, the environment surrounding them, and the cosmic conditions under which they develop. This afterglow model also yields specific predictions regarding the behavior of afterglow afterglows in both the exponential and adiabatic decay phases. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of absorption within the model, we derive the afterglow spectrum, which exhibits a power law behavior with an exponent of 1.5 immediately following the burst, and 2 at later stages, with the presence of a thermal component emerging in the latter case. This is supported by the results of extensive numerical simulations. By comparing our model with extensive observational data, we find that afterglow afterglows consistently exhibit a power law spectral index of 2, with the possibility of it being 1.5 in certain exceptional cases. This model also provides the foundation for understanding the rapid variability observed in some afterglows. We propose that afterglow afterglows may serve as cosmic tools for investigating the properties of the high-energy universe at various distances. This model has been made available as a interactive online resource. We have applied this model to the specific case of Gamma-Ray Burst 180720A, with the resulting predictions being consistent with the observed data. This model has implications for the study of afterglow afterglows in all wavelengths, from radio to high-energy gamma-rays. This model has the potential to be applied to other astrophysical phenomena, such as supernovae and pulsar winds. This model has been developed into a set of easily extensible and modifiable Python codes, with the underlying mathematical framework being detailed in the appendices. This model has been tested against extensive numerical simulations, with the results being compared to the predictions made by the model. As energy efficiency continues to top the list of priorities for mobile devices, a new challenge emerges at higher performance levels, where speed begins to surpass energy savings benefits. This paper introduces a novel, performance-energy optimization problem aimed at finding the most energy-efficient CPU frequency below a given throughput threshold within a mobile application's execution timeframe. We develop a precise mathematical representation of this problem and leverage convex optimization techniques to create an effective solution method. To validate our approach, we employ real workload data and observe an average frequency reduction of 30% with minimal performance degradation. Furthermore, our approach can be integrated into existing mobile operating system frequency scaling mechanisms with minimal modifications, offering a simple and lightweight solution. Ultimately, our research demonstrates a promising path for exploring a previously unexamined area of CPU frequency optimization. We open-source our research framework, known as HyperDegrade, to the mobile research community.

This discovery builds on a prior finding by the second listed author, and our method also offers a alternative proof of that result. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that this process can be applied to create a sequence of 1-cocycles associated with long knots, each resulting in a distinct order three Vassiliev invariant. The generated invariants exhibit connections to the IVC invariants and the 1-cocycle of a long knot. We also explore specific cases and demonstrate that in these instances, the generated invariants can be simplified to familiar forms. The process of producing these invariants from 1-cocycles is systematic, and we propose that this method can be utilized to create an infinite set of distinct order three Vassiliev invariants from any given 1-cocycle. The method we developed is then applied to create an order three 1-cocycle from the Dehn twist, and we further investigate the properties of the resulting invariant. In collaborative systems with multiple autonomous agents, optimal performance can often be achieved by having agents take on specific tasks that play to their individual strengths. In Federated Learning, models are trained across multiple parties without being centralised. This method overcomes issues related to data anonymization, encryption, and hefty data transfer costs. However, securing the process against malicious participants who feed manipulated data to the system has long been a challenge. While attacks on FL models that learn horizontally have been well-documented, research on attacks involving manipulated data for vertical FL, where features are learned across different dimensions, has been limited. This study presents not one but three novel attacks on the FL training process for vertical learning - one that deceives the model about the mean and two that make the model misjudge the data distribution. These attacks are practical, data-driven, and undetectable. When testing these attacks on real datasets, we found they were effective and comparable to more complex machine learning-based attacks. These attacks are simple to implement and rectify existing FL protocols to prevent them would demand a complete system redesign. Nonetheless, we propose a straightforward protocol modification that makes these attacks pointless. This study highlights the dangers of FL security being overly optimistic due to inadequate testing protocols. In addition, we provide a real-world example of such attacks on a banking system. Finally, we outline possible research avenues for those interested in delving deeper. This study was conducted in collaboration with a leading banking institution. In our study, we demonstrated how any group representation can be constructed from the representation of a subgroup in a base group. We achieved this by establishing a connection using the wreath product. A specific example is given where we generate the representation of the symmetric group S3 through the wreath product of a base group with a permutation representation. We then break down the process into its fundamental components called the Cartesian partition method. To accuracy in Word Sense Discrimination (WSD), selecting relevant contextgloss pairs is crucial. However, due to the limited number of glosses, current methods may choose low-quality pairs that include misleading or irrelevant information, negatively impacting performance. To address this issue, we introduce a novel technique, pair-refining, which enhances contextgloss pairs by eliminating pairs containing contradictory or ambiguous information. To further compress the reduced set of pairs, we propose a linear model that weighs the importance of each pair based on its similarity to the target word's context. To evaluate our proposed approach, we conducted experiments on three datasets using a gloss-based WSD setting and found that, compared to the baseline approach, our method resulted in a 12% to 18% improvement in F1-score. Moreover, our analysis revealed that contextgloss pairs containing both accurate and inaccurate information can be beneficial for training neural network-based WSD models, leading to a 5% to 7% performance gain. To facilitate future research, we have made our code and a newly created Senses Gloss Dataset publicly available. This new dataset comprises approximately 13,000 contextgloss pairs for 30 different word senses. To demonstrate the practical applications of our approach, we conducted a case study on the medical domain, where our method successfully reduced contextgloss pairs by approximately 87% while maintaining a 90% accuracy threshold. This achievement is significant because it enables the use of BART for WSD without the need for a massive amount of gloss data, outperforming the state-of-the-art performance on the Charactrstcs dataset by 8%. Lastly, our analysis indicates that contextgloss pairs can be viewed as expert opinions, further solidifying their importance in WSD tasks. Research in physics, biology, and finance often involves analyzing dependent and non-identically distributed terms within a sequence. This study leverages the block Devonshire method to break down a general model of sequence-based deviations, yielding explicit analytical results that illustrate the generic principles governing deviations in dependent and non-identical sequences. When analyzing dependent sequences, the critical factor influencing deviations is shown to be the second derivative of the free energy, and its behavior determines whether deviations conform to the central limit principle or exhibit skewed distributions. When studying non-identical sequences, the model reveals that the standard reference distribution for deviations can be the free energy itself, and this is demonstrated in an analysis of the Devonshire model. Both models also account for the effects of finite sizes and temperature on sequence-based deviations. Furthermore, this study provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to specific biological sequences, such as genetic codes. As a concrete example, the standard reference distribution for deviations in genetic codes is computed, showing that the distribution of codon frequencies conforms to a specific power law that is influenced by the number of different codons present. This result can be interpreted as codons that are frequently used exhibiting smaller deviations than rare codons, and this phenomenon is observed across all living organisms examined. This study investigates how model performance is affected by a specific technique called K-fold cross-validation, particularly within the NLP domain. We explored various aspects of K-fold CV, including its composition, the number of times it's employed, and its relationship to model hyperparameters. To minimize predicted outcomes' variability, we established optimal K-fold CV parameters. When adjusting a standard RoBERTa-based question-answering model as an example, we discovered that using a 7-fold CV profile, applied only once, yielded the smallest performance dispersion when fine-tuning the model. This study provides a method for determining optimal K-fold CV parameters, thereby minimizing predicted outcomes' variability when tuning NLP models. We suggest it as a standard practice within the NLP community to ensure model performance generalization. Moreover, we outline possible avenues for integrating K-fold CV with other machine learning methods. Artificial Neural Networks have advanced significantly since their inception, and recent developments attribute this progress to sophisticated techniques employing large amounts of data. However, implementing such methods is impractical due to the limited resources available to many mobile devices, wearable technology, and some embedded systems. Yet, despite these challenges, there's growing interest in developing AI-powered portable devices. Neural networks can be made more efficient for these applications by using simple, lightweight frameworks consisting of a limited number of dedicated neurons. This survey explores current research in this area, examining various frameworks designed to expedite knowledge acquisition for portable devices via efficient learning algorithms and optimization techniques. We delimit our focus to two popular categories: (1) fixed-precision frameworks and (2) adaptive-precision frameworks. For each category, we examine different frameworks based on their underlying architecture, review scalable learning methods to enable efficient knowledge acquisition, and discuss several optimization techniques to enhance the performance of these small networks. Finally, we outline some promising but less explored areas in the field, including memristor-based neural networks, meta-learning, and transfer learning. By consolidating the current state of portable neural networks, this survey aims to provide a valuable foundation for future innovative developments. We also include some numerical results to guide practitioners in evaluating the performance of different frameworks and methods for small-scale neural networks. In essence, this survey serves as a comprehensive knowledge base for both seasoned researchers and newcomer academics in the field of portable neural networks. We anticipate this survey will inspire further advancements in this area and encourage interdisciplinary collaboration among experts from various fields. As such, we've made the survey results available under the Creative Commons license to facilitate widespread access and use. As the field of portable neural networks continues to evolve rapidly, this survey provides a timely snapshot of the current state of the art. We've included an appendix detailing some of the notation and terminology used throughout the survey to enhance clarity and facilitate easy understanding. As the field of portable neural networks is highly interdisciplinary, this survey is relevant to a broad audience spanning multiple fields, including but not limited to artificial neural networks, electronics engineering, biometrics, signal processing, physiology, wearable technology, embedded systems, bioinformatics, medical imaging, medical physics, medical engineering, biomedical signal processing, biomedical engineering, bioinformatics, medical informatics, medical robotics, medical optics, medical mechanics, biomechanics, biophysics, biometry, biostatics, biomanagement, biochemistry, bioengineering, molecular engineering, molecular biology, molecular biophysics, molecular chemistry, molecular mechanics, molecular optics

We introduce a new method that significantly accelerates the exact computation of maximum probability explanations (MPE) and constrained maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates in graphical models, by first conducting a brief function approximation that typically takes much less time than existing approaches. This brief approximation is achieved by restricting the local configuration to a limited set of neighboring variables, rather than considering all possible configurations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by analyzing all possible local configurations, and derive efficient algorithms to evaluate them. In particular, for tree-structured graphical models, we show that the evaluation of all possible local configurations is straightforward and only requires a constant amount of time. In contrast, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach for general graphical models by offering a significant improvement in computation time. Experimental results confirm that our method offers faster computation times than the current baseline for a wide range of real-world datasets. We also introduce a new initialization approach for the popular branch and bound algorithm used for constrained MAP estimation, and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments. The code for our method is available at https://github.com/ali-ghodsi-pc/BriefMF.

Web search engines like Google typically suggest personalized results based on users' search history, geographic location, and account information. While this customization aims to present more relevant results to users, it's unclear how much this personalization affects the discovery of new information. In a study, participants were given a mock Web search scenario with either generic or personalized search results and were then allowed to explore additional pages for a specified list of query terms. When comparing the results, it was found that users with generic search results found a significantly greater number of desired terms (around 65% more), discovered new information on their own with greater frequency, and explored more web pages. These findings suggest that Google's default web search settings may be preferable for users seeking novel information. Furthermore, this research highlights the potential for information overload resulting from web search personalization, as users become too enamored with the presented results and fail to explore further. In turn, this phenomenon could impede the uncovering of new, relevant information, leading to incomplete knowledge. In essence, it appears that web search personalization may lead to the omission of a substantial number of pertinent information (around 55% in this study). Nevertheless, more research is needed to validate these findings and explore the generalizability of this phenomenon across diverse information contexts. If confirmed, however, it has significant implications for both web search engine designers and educational approaches to guiding users through the process of web search. The underlying issue also bears a resemblance to the problem of "information blindness," where users become desensitized to certain types of information. In response, designers could incorporate web search features that encourage users to explore beyond the initial results page. Additionally, the phenomenon of web search personalization leading to information blindness may be minimized by educating users on effective search strategies, promoting a more critical approach to evaluating the presented results, and providing tips on how to expand their inquiry to the broader web. In essence, it's essential to recognize that web search personalization is just one aspect of a broader information-seeking context that also involves user behavior, web content, and search engine algorithms. Consequently, designing more effective information-seeking experiences requires a holistic approach that considers these interacting components. The study described herein represents the initial outcome of a broader research project aimed at further examining the implications of web search personalization for the discovery of novel information. Future work will involve conducting additional experiments as well as exploring the generalizability of these findings to diverse information contexts. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has a more complex structure than compared to two-dimensional motion estimation, and as such, necessitates extensive amounts of training data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method for self-guided flow estimation in three-dimensional animated scenes. This proposal leverages a unique metric learning framework that generates a representation where the distance between corresponding points is minimal, and the distance between extraneous points is maximized. This is accomplished through an innovative adversarial training technique that produces a latent space in which the distribution of genuine point pairs differs significantly from the distribution of non-corresponding point pairs. We further develop a robust evaluation metric that concentrates solely on the assessment of correspondences rather than the overall flow accuracy. This allows us to demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over the state-of-the-art approaches in various challenging scenarios, including real-world datasets captured using lidar technology. In soccer, players often prioritize regaining possession over scoring, especially in close games. Current soccer agent research focuses on simple 1vs1 scenarios, without exploring the complexities of timed periods and scoring goals. We've developed a soccer agent model using deep reinforcement learning, allowing it to navigate various game situations, including those with timed periods and scoring goals, by training it on a condensed version of the full game. To put our model's capabilities to the test, we created three challenging 1vs1 scenarios with varying time limits and simulated crowd support. Our results show that the model excels in all scenarios, consistently adapting its playing style to controlled timed periods and even exhibiting strategic crowd-aware behavior. Furthermore, we discovered that in challenging scenarios with limited time, agents tend to take risks in deep trouble. To address this, we proposed a simple modification aimed at reducing this behavior, which we validated through additional experiments. Our model's performance serves as a foundation for strategies in critical soccer scenarios, and its underlying methodology provides a versatile framework for solving related problems in similar time-dependent scenarios. All code used in this research is available at https://github.com/ghGruyere/SoccerDeepRL.

The use of correctors to eliminate spherical aberration in TEMs through diffractive means has been successful, and over 100 instruments feature such solutions. In contrast, there are only a few machines with programmable phase discs for refractive aberration correction. This study explores the feasibility of employing a programmable phase disc as a substitute for refractive aberration correction. A specific disc designed to correct for a Coherent X-ray Free-Electron Laser source was analyzed and found to be ineffective due to its limited precision. However, if higher precision is achieved in programmable phase discs, it's possible they could be an affordable and practical solution for refractive correction, offering advantages over traditional solutions. Nonetheless, the challenges posed by the unique requirements of TEMs, including the need for precise control over disc changes and temporary phase discs for monochromated TEM, cannot be overlooked. Ultimately, the integration of programmable phase discs into TEMs has the potential to provide more flexible and cost-effective aberration correction.

The theory of superradiance suggests that rotating black holes or compact objects can create a pattern of oscillations in surrounding fields and matter. This phenomenon leads to the formation of a series of discrete modes of oscillation that align with the axis of rotation. As matter falls into the black hole, it loses energy and spins in sync with these modes. If an extremely light particle, such as an ultralight boson, is present in the surrounding field, it may also become entangled with the black hole's spin and its own corresponding mode of oscillation. In such a case, the energy and spin of the black hole will decrease in discrete steps that correspond to the energy of the ultralight boson. If an ultralight boson has a mass less than $10^{-12}$ eV, its oscillation modes could persist for the age of the universe. By analyzing the spin of massive quasars, we find that their spins are likely best described by a single distribution. Using this information, along with models of accretion and black hole formation, we can test the hypothesis that ultralight bosons exist by examining the superradiance modes in quasars and other similar objects. If confirmed, this would mark the discovery of a new fundamental particle with an unknown nature. Until then, we can constrain its properties based on the characteristics of quasars. Specifically, we find that the most likely distribution of quasar spins rules out ultralight boson masses less than $2.5 \times 10^{-13}$ eV. Additionally, if the distribution of quasar spins is shaped by a particular mechanism, then the corresponding ultralight boson may have a specific mass that could be determined through further analysis. In such a case, the minimum possible mass of the ultralight boson would be approximately $3.3 \times 10^{-13}$ eV. On the other hand, if the distribution of quasar spins is random, then the corresponding ultralight boson may have a broader mass range that could extend into the axion regime. In such a scenario, even if the distribution of quasar spins is random, we would still expect to find a peak in the number of quasars with specific mass combinations that align with the energy of the ultralight boson. Quantum linear algebra applications pose significant challenges for noisy intermediate-scale quantum technology. Despite this, there are particular algebraic transformations beneficial for future quantum systems. We introduce NISQ-HHL, a flexible framework to convert various linear algebra algorithms into forms suitable for noisy intermediate-scale quantum technology. As a proof-of-concept, we modified the Hamiltonian Linear Algebra Library to accommodate noisy intermediate-scale quantum capabilities and established that our version yields tangible performance gains for future machines. Specifically, we observed a 5.5 times improvement in execution time for a 4-qubit quantum application. To accommodate diverse quantum systems, NISQ-HHL allows users to create customized portfolios from pre-built qubit bundles, thereby enabling optimal resource utilization for noisy intermediate-scale quantum technology. Quantum developers can leverage our framework as a starting point and tailor NISQ-HHL to their specific needs. The modified Hamiltonian Linear Algebra Library, complete with usage guidelines and instructions for compiling and executing programs, is available open-source.

This article uses combinatorial and probabilistic methods to analyze the structure of the set of natural number-valued parking functions, which are represented as left ascents in a permutation of the numbers 1 through n. For a fixed positive integer n, we investigate the distribution of these ascents and determine the average first ascent location. Additionally, as n approaches infinity, we examine the structure of the set of parking functions for large n and its relationship to the interval (n-1, n+1). Specifically, we show that the ratio of this interval to the set of parking functions approaches one, and we can reinterpret this result using stochastic processes. Furthermore, we derive explicit formulas for the number of parking functions with a given first ascent location and discuss connections to Dyck paths and lattice paths. Lastly, we introduce a generalized version of parking functions associated with the positive real numbers, for which we determine the distribution of first ascent locations and establish an invariance property under a stochastic process.

We investigate the production of same-flavor Drell-Yan lepton pairs in a next-to-leading order precision in QCD framework for third-generation vector leptoquark models. After conducting an exhaustive search, we found that only the $SU(2)_L$ singlet and triplets vector leptoquark scenarios have been studied before, specifically with corrections up to order $\alpha_s$, for the process $q\bar{q}\to \ell^+\ell^-$ with $\ell = \ell_{3}$. Our research expands on this by calculating an accurate value for the $K$ factor at various leptoquark mass instances. Furthermore, we establish a relative importance of NLO corrections to $K$ factors which range from 20% to 50% with contributions from $V$ and $G$ components displaying opposing tendencies as the leptoquark mass increases from 400 GeV to 3 TeV. Additionally, we provide our results for the $K$ factor at a specific energy regime relevant to the LHC with 13 TeV. Lastly, our findings agree with existing data for the $SU(2)_L$ singlet case but also enable calculation extensions including for the $SU(2)_L$ triplets with second-generation lepton flavor components which we found to be negligible. Nonetheless, we do suggest incorporating third-generation jet fusion processes which we found to be insignificant but technically relevant processes. Moreover, we developed and reviewed relevant vector leptoquark Lagrangian terms and provided detailed derivations for the $K$ factor equation. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates physics-based uncertainty estimation in conjunction with multimodal learning to create a robust tool for imaging at reduced doses while accommodating acquisitions outside of their distribution. Compared to standard baselines, our model's capabilities in handling low-dose scans with altered protocols were significantly improved in a phantom study. Moreover, in a clinical setting with lung cancer patients, our model's performance in imaging at reduced doses was comparable to existing standards. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper delves into the connection between centering theory and a related concept called the given-new distinction, and further explores the link to the coreference resolution task. In this task, computers attempt to identify connections between words within a text with the aim of improving comprehension. Despite the potential utility of centering theory for understanding the coherence in texts, little research has been conducted on integrating it into the coreference resolution task. This paper presents an explicit integration of centering theory into the framework of neural coreference resolution. To evaluate this integration, the authors created a new metric that assesses the relationship between the predicted coreference relations and the perceived connections suggested by centering theory. This metric revealed a connection between the coreference resolutions predicted by the model and the connections it should exhibit according to centering theory, although this connection varies depending on the text. To better understand this variation, the authors conducted a simple analysis of the models' performance in relation to the complexity of the texts. This research demonstrates the practical utility of integrating centering theory into the coreference resolution task, and further suggests that such integration could provide insights into the underlying structures of texts. In addition, the authors open-source the metric developed in this research to facilitate further exploration of the coreference resolution task. This research was conducted as part of a larger project aimed at developing a more comprehensive understanding of the coherence in texts. This project, known as Coherence Analysis via Reference Resolution, seeks to create a general framework for analyzing the coherence in texts by studying the coreference resolution task through the lens of various linguistic theories. This research can be found at the project website, along with the code for the proposed approach and the metric developed in this research. This code is compatible with the popular BERT neural network architecture, although the authors note that the proposed approach can be used with other neural network architectures as well. This research was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. The metric dimension of a graph has been a well-studied concept with numerous applications. We introduce a new parameter, called the shortened metric dimension, which is a variation of the classic metric dimension. This new parameter considers the number of nodes whose removal results in at least two distinct distances between any remaining pair of nodes. We examine the shortened metric dimension of various graph types, and investigate its relationship with the standard metric dimension. Furthermore, we provide lower and upper bounds for the shortened metric dimension in specific graphs, and analyze its behavior under graph operations. Lastly, we discuss the connection between the shortened metric dimension and other parameters, and explore its implications in certain specialized graphs. In the process, we also derive upper and lower bounds for the classical metric dimension. The study presented here offers novel contributions to the field of graph theory, particularly with regard to the shortened metric dimension and its associated parameters. The research also aims to provide a theoretical framework that can be applied to practical problems involving the metric dimension in fields like biology and robotics. The study's findings are also relevant to real-world applications where the metric dimension has practical uses, such as in molecular biology, search and rescue operations, and network topology. The research presented here can be extended further, and we outline some potential avenues for future investigation. We introduce DISCO, a novel counterfactual dataset comprising over 13,000 phrasal extracts from 1,500 instruction-following web pages. Unlike existing sources, we find that currently available counterfactual datasets prioritize factual accuracy over format variety and often replicate similar questions. In contrast, our collection showcases a broad spectrum of formats, including but not limited to lists, conversations, and descriptive paragraphs. To demonstrate the value of DISCO, we tailor BART to generate both intrinsically rewarding and extrinsically valuable counterfactuals by leveraging the diverse format landscape. Our results reveal that pre-trained language models like BART can effectively produce both simple and complex counterfactuals when evaluated against human judgements. Moreover, we show that BART can be finely tuned to achieve outstanding performance on both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation tasks, surpassing the performance of human annotators. The DISCO dataset is now available for public use.

The unique properties of Heusler compounds make them extremely interesting for spin-orbit coupled electronics and magnetic phenomena. Epitaxial Heusler films grown on graphene/sapphire substrates offer minimal lattice mismatch and rotational inaccuracy, allowing for nearly freestanding films with controlled spin-orbit interactions. However, determining the equilibrium epitaxial configuration of these films is crucial, as it affects their electronic and magnetic behavior. We have investigated the epitaxial configurations of epitaxial Heusler films on graphene/sapphire using first principles calculations. Our results show that by adjusting the film thickness and whether the films are grown on clean or hydrogen-terminated graphene, it's possible to switch between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. Furthermore, we have characterized the remote and van der Waals epitaxy modes in detail, identifying specific thickness and graphene termination requirements. Ultimately, our findings provide a framework for controlling the epitaxial configurations of Heusler films on graphene/sapphire, enabling optimized spin-orbit coupled phenomena and magnetic properties.

However, accurate diagnosis from lung sounds that contain background noise and are affected by body anatomy makes sound analysis challenging.  Machine learning models can categorize heart sounds with some success but require highly controlled input data which is not representative of real-world auscultation. The proliferation of wearable medical devices enables continuous health monitoring, but poses a significant challenge to data privacy due to the sensitive nature of biomedical data. This concern limits the sharing of data across institutions, hindering collaborative research. This challenge is compounded by the lack of large, high-quality biomedical datasets for machine learning model training. To address this, we present FedHealth, a framework that enables collaborative learning across institutions using federated transfer learning. FedHealth leverages data within individual institutions to train personalized models, which are then combined using a federated averaging method. This results in a centralized model that can be used for biomedicine applications without accessing raw data. We evaluate FedHealth using publicly available biomedical datasets and find that it outperforms non-transfer learning and federated learning approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates robustness to model sharing methods and dataset sizes. To facilitate scalable experimentation, we present a PyTorch implementation of FedHealth for biomedicine. To address concerns about data privacy, FedHealth ensures that biomedical data remains localized, and we evaluate the trade-off between data sharing and model accuracy. Finally, we discuss extensions to FedHealth, including using more advanced model sharing methods and incorporating bias correction techniques. This framework has numerous applications in biomedicine, including the analysis of respiratory sounds from COVID-19 patients.
