While the automation of software development has advanced Significantly, developing automated systems for processing existing software has been largely overlooked. This phenomenon can be explained by the traditional assumptions underlying software development automation efforts. Firstly, it is assumed that compiled code remains static and unchanging after its initial creation. Secondly, it is assumed that program execution serves solely to verify the program's correctness. In contrast, this paper argues that compiled code often undergos dynamic changes and that program execution should be used for more than just validation. We propose the term "autodidactic computation" to describe the automatic modification and refinement of large-scale programs through their execution. This concept is reflected in our research, which focuses on developing a framework for efficiently and effectively Integrating automated systems that process and refine large programs. We have applied this framework to create an advanced processor for Python programs, which can evaluate and modify live Python applications. This processor, in turn, has been used to address real-world challenges, including the compilation of Python virtual machines for embedded systems and the optimization of web application performance. Our research demonstrates that compiled code is not immutable and that program execution is not limited to validation tasks. Furthermore, we believe that the widespread adoption of autodidactic computation will depend on the availability of affordable and high-performance systems that can efficiently execute and modify compiled code. To this end, we propose the development of specialized hardware that can optimize and accelerate autodidactic computation. Our research has far-reaching implications that extend beyond the realm of software and influence fundamental concepts in biology, psychology, and education. In particular, we believe that our research has implications for the theory of autodidactic computation, which underlies the processes of learning and development in living organisms and complex systems. In essence, we propose the term "autodidactic process" to describe any process that involves the self-modification of its own intermediate products in pursuit of a long-term goal. Our research has also been influenced by the principles of the "generative theory of learning," which posits that all learning results from the self-reorganization of existing knowledge in response to experience. In conclusion, our research on the development of a Python processor that can execute and modify live Python applications has led to a deeper understanding of the concept of autodidactic computation and its widespread occurrence in biology, psychology, and education. This study tackles a control problem where the cost function is given by the supremum of a stochastic process with continuous paths, and we aim to minimize this cost while adhering to a specific boundary condition. Key aspects of the problem include identifying whether it's possible to toggle the process above or below a certain level, as well as determining the structure of the process's extremes and its relationship to the solution of the controlled system. Existing research provides insights into these aspects, and we build upon them to derive an optimal control strategy. Furthermore, this problem can be reformulated as a system of partial differential equations involving the process's expectation and the probability of it exceeding a certain level, and we demonstrate that this system is viscously consistent when the process's expected value is continuous. Lastly, we provide an example where the process's expected value is not continuous, and this leads to a system with a corner where the process's cost is determined by the probability of it exceeding a certain level, and this results in a system with a switch in its viscosity solution. This research was presented at the 2022 Applied Mathematics conference in Abu Dhabi.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by the gradual movement of supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies. As they move, they emit gravitational waves that PTA experiments can identify through precise measurements of their associated cosmic radio signals. In response to the need for more accurate detection methods, we created an advanced analytical tool that can replicate these signals for binary systems with elliptical orbits. In a comparison with existing models, our method showed comparable levels of accuracy at a significantly lower computational expense. The paper concludes with some thoughts on the interdisciplinary nature of the field and the need for more realistic network structures to advance the field. The feeble b-principle can be stated as follows: given a representation of submanifolds of one higher dimension than the input manifolds, if most embeddings of the input manifolds into the submanifolds result in mappings to the submanifolds, then there exists a way to map the input manifolds to the submanifolds while maintaining the same differential properties. Large-scale cardiac mechanics simulations involve solving partial differential equations with complex right-hand side terms, and are typically solved using iterative linear solvers. These simulations also require the computation of multiple linear systems, making the choice of preconditioner crucial for accelerating solutions. In this study, we examine and compare the effectiveness of multilevel preconditioners based on algebraic methods to solve a particular cardiac mechanics problem. A particular focus is given to the performance of these methods on high-performance computing platforms. We consider algebraic multigrid methods with Ruge-ASTAD and Bruto-Larson coarsening, Fulmer's multigrid, and Addridge's multilevel solver with multiple coarse grids. Our results show that despite its simplicity, the Fulmer solver achieves comparable performance to more complex methods, often outperforming other methods by 10-20% or more. Furthermore, the analysis extends to the computation of the Jacobian matrix's eigenvectors, demonstrating the efficacy of the Fulmer solver in this context. Our findings recommend the Fulmer solver as a suitable and efficient option for cardiovascular mechanics simulations involving thin structures. In these scenarios, the solver's performance can be further enhanced by employing more sophisticated coarsening techniques. Our research utilized the environment of the National Institutes of Health, specifically the Laboratory of Cardiovascular Diseases, and relied on the MOAB library for data management. Our code is available for public use under the terms of the GNU General Public License. Our study consisted of 12 test cases involving progressively larger problem sizes, ranging from 1,500 to 193,040 elements, with models representing real-world cardiac structures. Our analysis focused on the left ventricle models but our results can be applied to other models representing the heart and its surrounding tissues. Our findings suggest that the efficacy of our methods diminishes when beyond 193,040 elements due to the vast memory requirements. Our research identified the optimal solver parameters for MOOGLS, the multilevel solver developed by Addridge, which resulted in a 2-3 times improvement in memory usage with only a 10-20% slowdown in performance. A combination of varying permeability values, arranged randomly, can lead to the spread of a diffusing object being affected in complex ways, ultimately resulting in the demise of a straightforward Gaussian model. Researchers identified specific conditions where this diffusion behavior can take on the characteristics of both linear and quadratic trends, even in the absence of any external forces influencing it. By utilizing specialized mathematical techniques, the underlying random permeability values were effectively quantified and analyzed, revealing that this diffusion spreads in accordance with a specific power-law basis that is inherently linked to its natural dimensions. This discovery's implications are not limited to geological formations but also have relevance for the study of random movements within varying environments. A novel approach has been developed for modeling this type of diffusion, based on the original random permeability values, that can be both numerically and analytically validated. Determining the factors that influence the correlation between galactic star formation rates and mass are crucial for accurate predictions of future star formation. We analyzed a comprehensive dataset of 3500 galaxies to investigate the role of bulges in shaping the relationship between SFR and mass, particularly at high mass levels. For disk-dominated systems, we found that the decline of SFR with mass is gradual. However, in bulge-dominated galaxies, we observed a sharp increase in the ratio of bulge to total mass at high mass thresholds (thresholds vary based on galaxy type and whether the bulge is classical or pseudobulge). These thresholds fall within the range of masses previously thought to characterize pure bulge galaxies. We also discovered that the transition mass where the ratio of bulge to total mass begins to increase significantly varies based on whether the bulge is classical or pseudobulge (M200: 5.5 x 10 to the power of 10 for classical and 2.5 x 10 to the power of 10 for pseudobulge). Consequently, the turnover in the SFR to mass ratio at high masses is likely influenced by the formation of bulges. This is supported by historical imagery showing that many galaxies with high mass turnover without prominent central bulges do show spiral arm star formation indicating a connection to the mass of these regions. This is also consistent with N-body cosmological simulations that demonstrate the effect of bulge formation on the M-SFR relation. The role of bulges in shaping the M-SFR relation highlights the significance of distinguishing between classical and pseudobulge galaxies. This distinction is crucial for accurately understanding galaxy evolution and the associated chemical enrichment. This is particularly relevant given the recent discovery of a linear correlation between the mass of stars formed and the mass of the galactic bulge. This relation holds true for a wide range of galaxy masses, from the masses of dwarf galaxies to the masses of massive elliptical galaxies. Therefore, the chemical enrichment of galaxies may depend on the mass of their bulges rather than their total mass. This possibility is worth exploring in depth in the future. This study also highlights the importance of considering the spatial distribution of star formation within galaxies when analyzing their integrated SFR. This is particularly relevant for low-mass galaxies with concentrated star formation. This is supported by historical imagery showing that many low-mass galaxies with concentrated star formation do show a high mass turnover without central bulge formation indicating a connection to the mass of these regions. We conduct evaluations of sentiment words, a technique that assesses a language's sentiment based on a source language's annotated data, for 9 languages including French, Turkish, and Swedish. We discover that the method outperforms the baseline for 6 out of the 9 tested languages. Further analysis reveals that the approach excels particularly when the source and target languages differ significantly, as measured by their linguistic distance. Moreover, we find that sentiment assessment tends to overestimate the difficulty of a language when considering structural aspects. To enhance the methodology, we propose modifying the approach to include related languages in the sentiment analysis task, demonstrating that this modification yields a high success rate of 87% in accurately determining the sentiment of new sentences, and 9% to 21% improvements in the Inference Accuracy Score for five out of the nine tested languages over the baseline approach. Notably, this modification enables the technique to accomplish intrinsic tasks such as sentiment classification. We also explore using the technique for an extrinsic task, namely cross-lingual question answering. The code and model are available at github.com/salemt/xtsaa.

X-ray images contain rich information that can be used for predicting patient outcomes by analyzing the external manifestations of COVID-19.  To address the limited data challenge in modeling hospital admission with COVID-19, we propose collecting and labeling features from X-ray images that correlate with ICU admission decisions.  To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, we gathered and annotated a small dataset of 1000 COVID-19 X-ray images, categorizing each as Type I, II, or III based on lung injury patterns and combining them with patient data including age, gender, ICU admission status, and temperature levels.  We then trained multiple machine learning models using this small dataset to predict ICU admission from both clinical data and X-ray features, and evaluated their performance to establish a baseline for future large-scale studies.  We also explored the influence of lung injury patterns on ICU admission in our dataset and found that pattern Type II is the most frequent indicator of ICU admission among the three types.  To prepare for larger-scale analyses, we developed a standardized annotation guide to facilitate consistent labeling of features from X-ray images by multiple clinicians.  We also introduced a novel approach based on multi-task learning to predict ICU admission from both clinical data and X-ray features, and evaluated its performance using our small dataset.  To further increase the efficiency of this model, we leveraged a technique called efficient net and compared the performance of this model with the standard one using our small dataset.  To enhance the generalizability of our findings, we collected and annotated another independent dataset of 2000 COVID-19 X-ray images with corresponding clinical data, and validated the performance of our model using this additional dataset.  To increase the scalability of our model to larger datasets, we trained it using a technique called mixup and compared the performance of this model with the standard one using our combined dataset of 3000 X-ray images.  To explore the applicability of our model to real-world settings, we conducted a simulated study using our small dataset and various sample sizes to examine the influence of data quantity on patient outcome prediction and analyzed the results using a technique called network analysis.  To facilitate replication of our results, we open-sourced our model implementation on a public platform.  To prepare for real-world implementations, we discussed the challenges and potential solutions associated with scaling up our model to real-world settings and proposed a research agenda to address these challenges. We've performed an in-depth analysis of 83 galaxy clusters at high redshift (approximately 2.5 to 3.5) with the help of HST observations from the Frontier Fields.  This investigation focused on the early stages of galaxy cluster formation and development.  We discovered a significant population of galaxies in these clusters that are composed mainly of older stars and lack significant central supermassive black hole activity.  These galaxies are found primarily on the outskirts of the clusters rather than at their centers.  This pattern suggests that matter may be distributed irregularly within these clusters due to gravitational influence from their surrounding halos.  Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the distribution of these galaxies and the overall structure of the clusters they reside in.  This is characterized by clusters with irregular shapes and loose groups of galaxies.  These findings are consistent with the idea that galaxy clusters form and grow through the accumulation of irregular groups and massive clusters.  In response to this growth, galaxies within these clusters are gradually transformed through gravitational interaction and mass accumulation, leading to changes in their morphology and star formation activity.  This, in turn, may eventually give rise to bulge formation within these galaxies.  This theory is supported by numerical simulations of these clusters.  This is also reflected in the distribution of stars within these galaxies, with the older stars found in bulge-like structures on one side, and the younger stars on the other.  This asymmetrical distribution of stars within these galaxies provides valuable insights into their formation and development, with possible explanations for their creation linked to accretion of gas and dust during the early stages of the universe.  This is further supported by the discovery of similar irregular structures within the Milky Way galaxy. Recently published research indicates that solar proton events can be broken down into individual neutron flux components using neutron monitor readings from multiple locations. This method can recover original proton flux spectra even when data from only one or two locations is available even with current solar proton measurement techniques. However, recovering accurate proton flux spectra from just one location requires accurate information about atmospheric particle composition and solar proton energy distribution. Notwithstanding these challenges, prior studies have consistently shown that neutron monitor readings from multiple locations can be combined to obtain more accurate proton flux spectra. Conversely, decomposing neutron monitor data from just one location is more speculative and lacks concrete empirical evidence. In this study, we employed this approach to analyze data from November 7, 2004, when a significant solar flare emitted a massive energy burst that was detected across the globe but also caused considerable signal obstruction in some recordings. Consequently, we were able to reconstruct proton flux spectra at this event, which is notable for its unusually large energy release and rare neutron decompositions observed globally. Moreover, our analysis revealed unusually long atmospheric particle trails at higher altitudes and it is hypothesized that this could be a result of the massive energy release combining with the prevailing atmospheric conditions to create this phenomenon. Furthermore, our findings suggest that recovering proton flux spectra from just one neutron monitor location is feasible and can provide accurate results with the necessary corrections in place. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Moscow Space Research Institute.

If a massive exoplanet is ingested by its host star, angular momentum must be generated quickly to match the observed effect of increased stellar spin. We used numerical simulations to verify that this assumed angular momentum transfer occurs. When modeling a 0.5 solar mass star with 0.5 solar radii ingested exoplanates, we found that, within 10^4 years, the star's rotation accelerates as expected, with a resulting spin period of around 0.7 days. This predicted outcome supports the ingestion hypothesis, but we also suggest alternative angular momentum sources, potentially from planetary cores or magnetic field fluctuations, which could account for similar stellar spin behavior. Although unlikely, our study shows that the assumed hypothesis is plausible, but more research is needed to confirm its validity. The simulated state can be matched with observed stellar states, and we propose detecting this effect by studying ancient stellar remnants. The predicted spin periods of subgiant stars that have ingested exoplanets are also explored. The assumed hypothesis has a counterpart in the solar system, with angular momentum generated by Jupiter's rapid accumulation allowing the sun to continue rotating. The rapid dissemination of fake news poses a significant threat to global social stability and security. To combat this issue, technologies that can automatically detect false news are urgently needed. To address this challenge, this research presents a novel method that combines text, image, and video-based embeddings to create a unified feature representation for news articles. This representation serves as input to a meta-learning framework, which trains networks to effectively capture the underlying patterns of true and false news. To leverage context information, the method incorporates a neural process component that updates the learned networks to adapt to new data categories. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on multimedia datasets, with results showing that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in various settings. Furthermore, the methodology is applied to a real-world dataset containing COVID-19 news, and the findings are found to be consistent with those obtained using existing models. The code for this research is available open-source on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrfeng/MMFIND. Moreover, a dedicated website has been established to host additional results, along with guidance for replicating the experiments. The proposed technique has the potential to be scaled up for use in large-scale, real-world applications, with potential areas of employment in social media platforms, online news websites, and various institutions tasked with monitoring and combating the spread of false news. This research paper examines the conventional periodic conveyance equation proposed by Pipberger in 1967, with the aim of further analysis to facilitate computer simulation of cardiac cycles. We derived the anomalous equation for this conveyance model and investigated its properties. The results show that the periodic conveyance equation has anomalous components that are analogous to those found in blood flow models, with the exception of a constant term in the periodic conveyance equation. We also found that the anomalous term in the conveyance equation is related to the anomalous term in the blood flow equation, with a difference of 1. This relationship can be expressed as an exact differential equation. To validate the model, we compared its predictions with experimental data from a study on respiratory fluctuations in cardiac cycles during normal breathing. The model successfully replicated the effects of respiration on cardiac cycles despite some discrepancies in the timing of certain events. It is noteworthy that the conveyance equation is insensitive to the anatomy of the heart chamber, making it a more general model. We also explored the implications of the model for cardiac cycle regulation and identified two possible control mechanisms: one based on feedback from the end-diastolic volume and the other related to the time elapsed since the onset of diastole. The model predicts that cardiac cycles become more irregular as the time since diastole increased, with some discrepancies from this prediction observed in the experimental data. The proposed model provides a more comprehensive understanding of the blood conveyance equation and offers insights into the control mechanisms governing cardiac cycles. The related code is available online. The model's limitations and potential improvements are also discussed. The research paper concludes by outlining the scope for future extensions to the model. Such sets possess unique complementary autocorrelation properties, both in phase-shifted and unshifted configurations. This paper introduces the concept of polyphase Golay complementary sets with more general defining matrices and proposes a construction method for these sets based on combinatorial designs, specifically orthomorphs of the Reed-Solomon code and a particular type of difference set. This approach enables the creation of large-sized sets that exceed the limitations of previous construction methods. Furthermore, this work showcases specific instances of both small-sized and large-sized sets for both their individual phases and combined phases. Lastly, a particular case study is presented where the sets are constructed using the Reed-Solomon code orthomorph, and this is shown to be equivalent to a previously known method. This research also explores connections to existing systems and provides an apparatus for jointly generating multiple sets from a single source. We establish a connection between specific collections of subspaces in a linear series and the concept of divisors from algebraic geometry. This connection enables us to apply the Serre duality theorem to count the subspaces in a linear series that contain given subspaces. As a result, we derive an enumerative formula to calculate the number of lines contained within a cubic surface and satisfying additional specifications. This formula extends and refines earlier enumerative calculations from classical and modern sources. Additionally, we provide a straightforward proof of an enumerative statement initially confirmed by the works of Schubert and Peterson, among others. Furthermore, this approach simplifies and expands upon the application of the duality theorem to the enumerative proof of the identity $245 = 13 \times 19$ presented by Zariski. Similar techniques can be applied to calculate the number of lines that lie on a cubic surface and intersect specific surfaces at particular points. These surfaces can include lines, conic sections, and spherical surfaces. This generalization maintains its statistical interest when restricted to the scenario of lines intersecting a cubic surface at one point each. As such, we offer comprehensive enumerative data for this specific case. As a broader context, we outline the theoretical framework of the problem within the framework of homotopy theory. This involves defining a space called the configuration space and demonstrating how the enumerative data we calculated can be extracted from the knowledge of the Lefschetz number, in turn derived from the knowledge of the configuration space. A significant issue in using deep learning for medical imaging is the presence of contraindicative pathologic tissue. This challenge can be illustrated with the problem of using MRI for surgical planning. In this case, certain brain lesions can hinder the effectiveness of some neurosurgical procedures. As such, it's crucial to detect and avoid these lesions during surgery. However, training a deep learning model to automatically detect these lesions requires a large dataset that includes high-quality images of these lesions. Yet, such datasets are rarely available. To address this issue, we propose an unconventional approach where the model is trained to generate new brain images that show specific types of lesions. To accomplish this task, we developed a novel Progressive Variational Adversarial Auto-encoder model that can generate high-quality images in stages. Each stage focuses on either the low-resolution base image, the intermediate resolution image that exhibits the characteristic of the lesion, or the high-resolution image that accurately represents the lesion in question. Furthermore, we introduced a new evaluation metric that takes into consideration the spatial distribution of the lesion. Utilizing this metric, we showed that our proposed model outperforms competing alternatives. To demonstrate its practical applications, we used the model to simulate studies on brain biopsy, specifically on the presence of a particular type of glioma tumor. This was achieved by generating synthetic images that were indistinguishable from real images, as verified by a medical expert. This model has numerous potential uses, including but not limited to, generating synthetic data for biopsy procedures. In the process, we open-sourced the model, along with instructions on how to use it, under the name Cerebral Lesion Generator. This allows other researchers to build upon our work and facilitate collaborative progress. In addition, we contributed a comprehensive report on the model's performance at each stage, which can be found in the supplementary materials. This report is crucial in guiding further improvements to the model, specifically with regard to modifying the adversarial loss function in order to achieve more realistic generated images. This is especially important for evaluating the model based on standard evaluation metrics, which rely heavily on the similarity between real and generated images. To this end, we proposed a novel way to adapt the structural similarity index measure metric to evaluate the model's performance stage by stage. This is a significant contribution in its own right, as it enables the evaluation of deep learning models that generate images in stages. GP 2 is  an abstract syntax for graph programs incorporating nested scope rules, thereby enabling the definition of graph-to-graph and graph-to-string transformations. A GP 2 compiler has been developed, taking GP 2 representations as input and producing graph-to-graph rewrite rules in the RelNorm form of the WGP language. The enhanced GP 2 compiler expands upon its predecessor by incorporating several key features, including the capability to handle GP 2 definitions featuring negative application conditions within graph-to-graph transformation frameworks. Furthermore, it includes an optimization phase in its compilation process. The GP 2 compiler is implemented using the WGP compiler framework and is capable of generating executable WGP models from GP 2 definitions. Experimental evaluations conducted using a variety of real-world datasets reveal the compiler to be computationally efficient, outperforming the predecessor GP 2 compiler in terms of both execution time and memory consumption. The source code for the GP 2 compiler is made available as open-source software written primarily in the Scala programming language. The compiler's capabilities are demonstrated through applications in the fields of biology and finance. The GP 2 compiler provides a suitable example for teaching and learning the principles of graph transformation compilation, along with providing a practical tool for researchers and developers interested in graph transformation-based algorithms. The GP 2 test suite, comprising approximately 70 test cases, is also made available for validation purposes. The compiler's efficiency in processing complex datasets serves as a benchmark for future GP 2 compiler designs. The GP 2 compiler source code and additional documentation are available online at the following location: https://github.com/CompLerProject/gp2-compiler. The GP 2 compiler's performance, along with various experimental results and the underlying code, has been curated into a standalone IPython environment for ease of access and reproducibility. In recent years, there has been significant interest in constructing universal features that enable models to be adapted across multiple related tasks. This endeavor can be a promising strategy for tackling challenging data analysis problems involving either too many features or high dimensionality. Researchers have proposed various methods for automatic feature extraction from a given dataset, some of which can be classified into three main categories: linear transformations, nonlinear transformations, and neural network-based techniques. Although these methods can extract universal features for specific applications, they typically require a separate module for each individual task, including a network that has been trained specifically for that task. This can lead to several issues, including (1) the need for a large amount of data for each individual task, (2) the difficulty of incorporating prior knowledge about different tasks, and (3) the challenge of ensuring that the features extracted are both generalizable and of high quality. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel end-to-end framework called the Comparative Structure (CompStruct) that integrates multiple tasks into a single, unified network. This integrated network enables not only feature extraction but also a comparison among different tasks, allowing for the selection of the most relevant tasks and incorporating prior knowledge about each task. This prior knowledge can be provided in the form of a regularization term that is incorporated into the loss function of the network. This framework is both generalizable and of high quality, with applications across various challenging real-world data analysis problems. Moreover, this paper demonstrates the effectiveness of CompStruct through comprehensive experimental results on multiple datasets, including the MNIST, CIFAR, and VGG Face datasets. These results confirm that CompStruct outperforms state-of-the-art methods for both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction. This paper also presents detailed design choices for the network, including the architecture of the network, the loss function, and the regularization term, as well as a computational complexity analysis and a comparison with related methods. Finally, this paper concludes by identifying potential directions for further research, including the integration of transfer learning and the extension of CompStruct to tackle more challenging problems involving both high dimensionality and feature missing not reported. This may provide even better performance, as demonstrated in the experimental results presented in this paper. Working with nominal data poses specific challenges due to its ordinal nature lack of mathematical structure. Furthermore, combining nominal data with large dimensions presents an additional difficulty. To address these issues, a new method is proposed to perform dimension reduction using Group Lasso, first by converting the nominal variables into ordered weights, then by utilizing a sparsity-inducing Group Lasso technique with an L1 L2 penalty. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the method's performance and a real-world application is explored in the context of text messages. Results show that this approach outperforms the alternative method based on the popular Random Forest algorithm. Moreover, the proposed technique facilitates the interpretation of results by identifying the significance of specific categories within the nominal data. Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance on numerous knowledge-based tasks. However, the underlying premise that these models possess broad knowledge within their parameters has not been thoroughly substantiated. We contend that the ability of these models relies heavily on structured knowledge resources, specifically when dealing with large-scale knowledge requirements. To support this view, we was able to demonstrate that the performance of LLaMA, when employed for knowledge-intensive tasks, can be significantly improved when incorporating structured information from resources like Wikidata. Moreover, we found that both utilizing Wikidata and training the model on related text data is necessary to achieve optimal results. To facilitate further exploration of this discovery, we presented two evaluation frameworks that assess the model's ability to make use of structured knowledge and integrate disparate sources of information. These frameworks are intended to contribute to the development of a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between large language models and structured knowledge resources. To further advance this goal, we encourage the participation of research communities in refining the evaluation methods presented here. The code, model, and evaluation tools are available at https://github.com/thomsmith/ability.

High-resolution vector maps are gaining popularity due to their versatility in graphics rendering. In contrast to static raster maps, they can be easily updated and modified without loss of image quality. However, rendering these maps on limited-resource displays, especially with the increasing demand for compact head-up displays, poses significant technical challenges. In particular, anti-aliasing techniques, which smooth out image edges, can result in longer display update times. Therefore, we evaluated and optimized anti-aliasing strategies for rendering line junctions on vector maps, focusing on reduced computational overhead to facilitate seamless display refresh rates. Our analysis shows that by tailoring anti-aliased rendering techniques to specific map elements, we can minimize memory consumption and accelerate rendering, leading to a 30% decrease in display update times and a 25% reduction in memory usage. Furthermore, our research includes an in-depth analysis of the computational costs associated with popular vector map rendering libraries, including SVG, OpenGL, and Cairo. Our optimized anti-aliasing technique for line junctions is now available under the Apache Open Source License on GitHub. In addition, we provide recommendations for general anti-aliasing quality settings to balance performance and display aesthetics. In particular, we found that reducing the complexity of anti-aliasing techniques during map display can result in up to a 5 times decrease in display update times. In conclusion, our research focused on the critical issue of display refresh rates when rendering high-resolution vector maps, and we believe its findings are relevant to a broad range of graphics applications beyond head-up displays. In multi-channel speech processing, having more than one recording can be very
beneficial for both source separation and speech enhancement tasks. This paper
investigates individual channel speech improvement where two-channel recordings
are used to enhance the speech signal in one channel, given the other as aid.
We propose a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) to solve this
problem. The proposed network consists of two paths: the Convolution Recurrent
Network (CRN) acts as a encoder and decoder, while the other part generates an
external noise estimate. We investigate DPCRN in two-channel speech recording
scenarios and find it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally,
we explore two-channel telephony recordings and see that DPCRN also performs
well in real-world scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/parth07/DPCRN.

Tensor networks have distinct storage and computational requirements to describe physical systems, particularly for describing thermal states and time-evolving processes. In the study of 1D systems, tensors that represent local elements can be combined to capture the behavior of an entire system. However, constructing efficient tensor networks involves several challenges, especially when modeling complex thermal equilibrium situations and dynamic processes. We present a method for constructing efficient tensor networks based on a local representation of the thermal density matrix and a temporal evolution obtained via a quadratic interaction. This approach enables us to systematically derive tensor networks from the fundamental physical parameters of a given model. As a result, we obtain networks with precise and local tensors that accurately represent thermal states and temporal evolution derived from a quadratic interaction. Furthermore, the tensors that comprise these networks allow for the efficient computation of local physical quantities through a combination of the canonical form of the thermal density matrix and the temporal evolution obtained via a quadratic interaction. As a specific application, we develop a local tensor network to describe the thermal equilibrium and temporal evolution of a bosonic Dicke model, which is particularly challenging to handle with conventional numerical methods. Our local tensor network yields an exact representation of the thermal density matrix and temporal evolution derived from a quadratic interaction, obtained by applying a canonical form to the thermal density matrix. This is demonstrated by comparing the physical quantities obtained from the local tensor networks with those obtained via conventional numerical methods, which shows that they converge to the same results for both thermal equilibrium and dynamic processes. This is particularly evident when examining the local expectation values of the number operator, the interaction operator, and the Wigner function. Consequently, our local tensor networks provide a precise and efficient method for describing thermal states and temporal evolution derived from a quadratic interaction, which can be achieved through the application of a canonical form to the thermal density matrix. This is accompanied by a supplementary material that contains the local tensor networks in the canonical form for additional models, including the Jaynes-Cummings model, the Tavis-Cummings model, and the linearly coupled Bose-Bose and Bose-Fermi models. This demonstrates that our method is universally applicable to a broad class of models. The storage requirement for these networks is directly proportional to the number of local elements rather than the number of lattice sites in the system, which makes them particularly useful for modeling dynamic processes involving a small number of local elements, as well as for storing the data for the thermal density matrix and temporal evolution derived from a quadratic interaction. Many real-world situations involve adapting models to new, unseen data without access to the original training set. This challenge is particularly relevant for various out-of-distribution generalization tasks, including, but not limited limited to, detecting new malware types and identifying unknown speakers. In such cases, only the output of a black-box model is typically available, with no access to its underlying training data or model parameters. This research explores the possibility of transferring knowledge from a black-box model to enhance performance on these types of tasks without retraining the model. We introduce a novel approach called Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer via Optimization (ZOTO), which leverages the derivatives of the output with respect to inputs to effectively expand the model's coverage to new data without seeing the original training set. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method across a range of scenarios, including both synthetic and real-world data, and show that it outperforms several baseline methods. ZOTO's versatility allows it to be applied in various contexts, including but not limited to, enriching classification boundaries and detecting epistemic uncertainty. We also provide a detailed cost analysis of ZOTO and identify suitable activation functions to minimize this cost. Furthermore, we introduce a new speaker recognition challenge task and detail our methodology for transferring knowledge to it. This paper proposes a metric function that can be used to detect errors in Pulse-Audio Codes (PAC). When a PAC code is affected by noise, the metric identifies the bit positions where the code and the corrupted signal diverge significantly. We argue that this measure helps in calculating the probability that a PAC code remains unaltered under interference from signals in a given environment. To calculate this probability, we introduce a mathematical model that accounts for the non-coherent noise PAC codes are designed to resist. This model enables the derivation of a closed-form formula for the error correction probability of PAC codes, specifically the probability that a PAC code of length $n$ remains accurate in the presence of up to $k$ errors, i.e., $P_d(n,k)$. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the calculation of this probability for a given PAC code and shows that this code has a high probability of remaining unaltered when exposed to certain types of noise. Furthermore, we establish lower and upper bounds for $P_d(n,k)$ using established mathematical inequalities which can be effectively determined using both numerical and graphical methods. These bounds can be applied to evaluate the accuracy of PAC codes in various environments. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between PAC codes and another error correction concept known as Hamming codes, and identify distinct differences between these codes. In particular, we found that the error correction probability of the Hamming codes discussed in literature does not match the formula derived in this paper, indicating a need for a new analysis of these codes. Similarly, this study also examines the error correction probability of the PAC codes with an odd number of bits, which has not been explored before. Lastly, we propose a method for constructing PAC codes with an even number of bits, which has the potential to significantly lower the noise resistance threshold of these codes. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the error correction properties of PAC codes, which can be used as guidelines for future research into these codes. Moreover, we believe that the approach used in this study could be applied to investigate the error correction properties of other code types. Lastly, we invite the scientific community to engage in a dialogue regarding this research and offer suggestions on how it could be improved. This study also offers a practical application of the noise resistance performance of PAC codes to the error correction of Pulse-Carrier Codes. This issue makes standard epsilon-greedy methods costly because of the extensive set of possible words in the source language. To address this challenge, researchers have experimented with techniques that treat the action space as continuous, but this approach isn't entirely suitable because the action space is discrete and the reinforcement learning model needs to output an integer. We explore two parametric models that handle this problem: a basic approach using a fixed vocabulary filter and a more complex technique using neural skimbers. Our results show that both methods outperform the standard epsilon-greedy approach and the continuous approximation. Additionally, we find that using neural skimbers leads to improved performance when the reward function is difficult to learn. A system consisting of a qubit and a reservoir, connected to two separate drives, provides an ideal setting for such investigations. When the system is driven by a periodic force, in a closed system, it would cycle through the same thermodynamic processes as the drive, but in an open system, the behavior is more complex due to the system's interaction with the environment. We explore how the repeated application of certain differential operators to a biharmonic hypersurface in the Euclidean space can lead to the hypersurface being minimal. Specifically, we investigate the implications of a hypersurface satisfying the following conditions in the Euclidean space: it is biharmonic, satisfies the covariant Laplacian being harmonic, and its mean curvature satisfies a specific differential equation. These conditions result in the hypersurface being minimal when applied to it three times, providing a new proof of a previously known result. Additionally, we derive three distinct meanings for the term "regularity" in the context of a hypersurface and provide examples of hypersurfaces exhibiting these different regularity types. Furthermore, we provide specific examples of hypersurfaces that satisfy the aforementioned conditions in the Euclidean space and in a space of constant curvature. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between these conditions and the concept of weak biharmonic hypersurfaces. Given any irrational number p divided by an irrational number q, we define a subset S of the integers as being p/q-identifiable in the context of a given system of linear equations with integer coefficients. This property holds if the subset S contains all integers that can be represented in the form (Ap+B)/q, where A and B are integers from a specific, clearly definable group of possible coefficients in the system of linear equations. Our research delves into the statistical characteristics of p/q-identifiable sets within a randomly generated ensemble of systems of linear equations. We demonstrate the prevalence of p/q-identifiable sets among all systems of linear equations and quantify this prevalence as (1-delta) times a fixed constant, where delta represents an arbitrarily small positive value. Furthermore, we investigate how the prevalence of p/q-identifiable sets changes in response to variations in q and p. In addition, we establish that the majority of systems of linear equations exclude a specific, definable subset of the integers that are divisible by a particular number, and we determine the measure of this excluded subset as (1-delta) times a fixed constant. We accomplish this for any given number, regardless of it being rational or irrational. In the course of our analysis, we establish a probabilistic criterion that can be applied to any system of linear equations with integer coefficients and provides insight into the distribution of the coefficients within the system. We also develop a statistical approach to analyzing the distribution of the coefficients within a system of linear equations. This analysis enables us to apply our methods to systems of linear equations with coefficients drawn from a hypercube distribution. We demonstrate that the prevalence of p/q-identifiable sets among systems of linear equations with coefficients drawn from a hypercube distribution is essentially the same as the prevalence of p/q-identifiable sets among systems of linear equations with coefficients drawn from a uniform distribution. In the task of arranging random words into coherent sentences, prior research has shown that language models can often generate plausible sentences without the aid of additional training. To further understand the role of pre-trained language models in this process, we explored the capabilities of BART in arranging word groups. Our findings indicate that BART typically produces high-quality sentences when given groups of words that form coherent sentences on their own. However, when given disjoint sets of words each representing a coherent sentence, BART struggles to combine them into a meaningful sentence. We discovered that the most effective approach is simply using BART to arrange the words due to its high baseline performance, and that while more sophisticated methods may generate more diverse sentences, they do not significantly outperform this baseline in terms of grammatical correctness as evaluated by human assessors. We also examined the various BART models and found that using a larger model does not necessarily lead to improved performance. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes using network analysis has been previously unfeasible. This study presents a statistical analysis of the Forsage pyramid scheme, using public blockchain data to investigate its statistical characteristics and how they change over time. Our research finds that Forsage participants follow a power-law distribution when investing in different levels of the network, with a high degree of consistency across various time periods and geographic locations. This unusual finding challenges existing assumptions about power-law behavior in financial contexts, where participants typically follow a log-normal distribution. Furthermore, our data reveal that Forsage operators employ deceptive strategies, exploiting vulnerabilities in the scheme's design to disguise their true identities and profit from the scheme. This study uses Forsage data to also examine pyramidal schemes with fake withdrawals, showing that they generate networks with characteristic patterns of decreasing investment at higher levels. Our analysis highlights the difficulty of detecting such schemes, as they closely resemble legitimate investment networks. Our research utilized simple statistical models to simulate the behavior of participants in these schemes, providing insights into their underlying mechanics and revealing that they often adhere to specific mathematical principles, such as the 60-30-10 rule, where 60% of participants occupy the outer network, 30% form closed loops, and 10% reside in the inner network. Our findings suggest that pyramidal schemes often exhibit robust patterns of behavior, making them challenging to disguise as legitimate financial networks. This study provides a statistical framework for analyzing similar schemes in the future, using only publicly available data from blockchain transactions. Our research into Forsage also reveals that, unlike traditional pyramid schemes, it allows participants to withdraw their investments, which enables us to examine its network under different withdrawal conditions, revealing that it generates networks with characteristic patterns of instability and fragility in response to changes in withdrawal terms. Our analysis provides a simple simulation-based model for simulating the behavior of these networks, along with various modifications, and our data show that Forsage networks often adhere to the principles of the "prison experiment," where participants conform to social norms and behave responsibly to maintain social cohesion. Generative adversarial networks have been successfully applied to text creation by competing between a generator producing high-quality data and a discriminator accurately differentiating between genuine and fabricated data. Our investigation focuses on two key discoveries to enhance the effectiveness of GANs in creating short texts, namely that (1) dense models are not optimal for classification tasks, especially when there are significant class imbalances, and (2) a true adversary is characterized by being difficult to saturate, not just being difficult to train. Based on these findings, we propose SparseGAN, a framework that incorporates two key features: (1) employing sparse models in both the generator and discriminator, and (2) implementing a progressive learning approach to ensure the discriminator is consistently challenged. Our proposed framework surpasses the performance of existing methods in text creation tasks. When generating text, we incorporate a variety of profiling aspects to ensure the created text aligns with submitted profiles. To evaluate our method, we conducted experiments using datasets for creating neutral texts and found that SparseGAN delivers superior performance to the current state of the art. When creating biased texts, we modified the framework to suit the specific text creation task, and our method was found to be highly superior to the current standard. Another approach involves analyzing how animals select habitats, which can also inform population size estimates. We then applied and evaluated this method on real capture-recapture and resource selection data from African elephants in Kenya. Our results showed that the "rredlist" package accurately estimated population size and provided reliable predictions of density and abundance under different survey designs. Given a non-abelian group G with a faithful irreducible representation of degree greater than 1 in the vector space V, we explore the behavior of G-action trajectories on V. Our primary objective is to classify the distinct trajectories of G's conjugation action within the set of unitary operators on V. As a result, we obtain specific trajectory types and their corresponding algebraic structures. In particular, if all unitary operators in V share the same conjugacy class, we establish that G's action is equicontinuous, resulting in the compactness of the unitary operator space divided by the conjugacy relation. Additionally, we identify a connection between the action's trajectory type and the character table entries via a formula derived from the matrix entry distribution along the trajectories. Furthermore, we provide a solution to the Tetrathlon Problem by demonstrating that the cyclic group S3 action on the V space is transitive if and only if the representation degree is 3. We also examine how the trajectories behave under the combination of two non-abelian groups and include an associated criterion for action continuity. Our research methods involve combining representation theory, operator theory, algebraic geometry, number theory, and analytical number theory. We hope this work will facilitate interactions between these areas and spark further discoveries. Our findings are also applicable to the Enveloping Group scenario. We explore the capabilities of small-world networks to facilitate accurate estimation across large systems compromised by malicious entities. In this study, we demonstrate that small-world networks with a central hub can effectively resist the detrimental effects of a small number of treacherous participants, even when these malicious actors have unlimited resources and can engage in deceptive tactics with ease. Conversely, we also investigate the minimum number of trustworthy participants required to ensure the accuracy of the estimation, finding that it scales exponentially with the number of compromised nodes in the network. Moreover, we propose a practical algorithm that leverages local coordinates to achieve resilient estimation capabilities, and through simulations, we validate the effectiveness of this approach across various network configurations. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis to support our algorithm's efficacy, concluding that its accuracy is directly proportional to the ratio of reliable nodes to the total number of nodes in the network. In the course of our research, we also encountered an interesting estimation problem that can be solved using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. The research presented herein contributes to the field of small-world networks, providing novel insights that can be applied to real-world scenarios, as well as offering a practical estimation solution using Monte Carlo methods. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.  This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term traffic conditions in congested areas using simple combinatorial methods.  A binary system of "congested" or "uncongested" conditions is estimated for individual detectors and aggregate road segments based on real-time data from mobile probes.  Probing data from major roads yields more accurate estimates than side streets due to higher speeds and more frequent probing.  Combining the estimates of individual detectors into segment-level estimates poses a challenge, as it involves accounting for the contributing probes and their respective weights.  This study proposes a weighted estimator using the probability of encountering a probe within a specific distance from the beginning of the segment as its key component.  The weighted estimator outperforms a basic estimator with no weighting, as it prioritizes probes that are likely to provide more accurate information about the start of the segment over those that offer information further downstream.  The effectiveness of the weighted estimator is demonstrated through empirical analysis, as it yields higher accuracy than the basic estimator for both major and side streets.  The study also explores alternative weighted estimators, as it shows that the probability of encountering a probe within a specific distance from the beginning of the segment serves as a reliable proxy for its weight. A systematic review of cometary spectra containing molecular cations is presented, with a focus on those involving oxygen. Knowledge gaps in the cometary data set are identified, particularly in regards to cationic molecules featuring an oxygen-oxygen bond, which have been largely uninvestigated. Furthermore, there is a lack of information on the neutral counterparts of these cationic molecules, limiting the understanding of their formation and destruction processes in cometary atmospheres. To move forward in this area, it is essential to revisit and re-analyze existing cometary spectra using modern spectroscopic models, as well as to conduct observations targeted at the missing oxygen-containing cationic species. By doing so, a more comprehensive understanding of the physical and chemical processes occurring in cometary environments can be gained. To facilitate new observations, a list of targeted cationic species is provided, with suggestions for improving the detection of oxygen-containing molecular cations in cometary spectra. The inclusion of neutral counterparts of these cationic species in photochemical and dynamical comet models is also advocated, in order to gain a more complete view of the interactions between cometary atoms and molecules, as well as their solar and internal influences. The knowledge presented in this review is relevant to ongoing and future cometary missions, including the ESA Rosetta mission, the NASA Stardust mission, the NASA CAHTERINE mission, the JAXA Smart-1 mission, as well as ground-based telescopic observations employing spectrographs. The opportunities and challenges associated with these initiatives are discussed, along with the availability of relevant spectroscopic knowledge, modeling tools, and observational strategies. To facilitate this process, researchers created tools that can verify the correctness of these tools relative to a particular theorem proving system, using that system's original proofs for similar theorems. However, each verification tool has its own proprietary proof format, making it difficult to compare their results. To address this issue, the developers of the Alethe system introduced a flexible and open framework for representing and comparing the results of these verifications. Although Alethe is primarily designed to facilitate comparisons between the outcomes of different verification tasks, its capabilities extend to evaluating the impact of various theorem proving systems' strategies on problem solving, as well as analyzing the relationships between different mathematical theories. To demonstrate the versatility of Alethe, we present an analysis of the strategies employed by three distinct theorem proving systems, using abstractions of well-known mathematical theories. Furthermore, we provide a brief overview of Alethe's components, including its parser, translator, and evaluator, as well as a discussion on the opportunities and challenges associated with sharing proven statements. To facilitate replication, we made Alethe available as an open source project under the terms of the BSD license. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is observed with significant absorption in its Hubble Space Telescope spectrum. A comparison with other spiral galaxies reveals unusually strong absorption in UGC 8839, particularly in the 2500-3000 Angstrom range where the 2500 Angstrom feature is absent. This distinctive spectral characteristic is thought to be caused by a super-saturated Lyman line spectrum originating from a vast, luminous halo. However, modeling this phenomenon is challenging due to its complexity and the limited availability of relevant observational data. As a result, a new theoretical model is developed to reproduce the 2500 Angstrom feature by post-processing a hydrodynamic simulation of a galaxy with a $10^{12}$ solar mass halo. The resulting model exhibits a 2500 Angstrom equivalent width that is 3 times greater than typically observed in spiral galaxies and is influenced by both the halo's extent and the central bulge's contribution. Nonetheless, despite its limitations, this single-model scenario is relatively successful in replicating the 2500 Angstrom feature's strength observed in UGC 8839. As such, it is now known as the "hyper-constant" case. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 100 actions per second, largely because of how they process language.
Our new benchmark, TextWorldExpress, shatters this barrier by leveraging specialized hardware and optimized code to process text-based games at incredible rates, achieving a record 1 million actions per second.
To demonstrate the potential of this platform, we organized a competition where top-ranked agents on the TextAdventure League website were put to the test in TextWorldExpress.
The results reveal that the top-performing agents, previously victorious in the TextAdventure League, failed to excel in TextWorldExpress due to issues like slow performance and inconsistencies in reward systems.
In contrast, a custom agent designed for TextWorldExpress showed significant improvements in both speed and performance.
Our analysis highlights the importance of optimizing code for high-performance text-based games and highlights areas where existing agents can improve.
TextWorldExpress is available online, awaiting submissions from top-ranked agents on the TextAdventure League website.

The results presented hold under the assumption that the dimensionality of the matrices is greater than 2. We explored a stylized model where two populations, one production and the other, evolve in a co-dependent manner through genetic algorithms. We found that in a model based on Nash equilibrium, a constant population size led to an equilibrium state, whereas a changing population size led to periodic behavior. Next, we varied the model by introducing reproduction mechanisms derived from genetic variation, including random, gradient-based, and tournament methods. Our key observation showed that when the population size was constant, the population converged to a Nash equilibrium. To broaden our findings, we introduced a range of other reproduction mechanisms, many of which resulted in the population converging to the Nash equilibrium with the exception of: when noise was high in the population, when there was little genetic variation, when the population size was too small, and in cases of skewness, all of which prevented convergence to the Nash equilibrium. Lastly, we scaled up the model to a market with multiple goods and found that it converged to a multi-Nash equilibrium. To address this, researchers have been exploring ways to make convolutional neural networks resistant to hardware faults. Previously studied methods primarily focused on training resilient models using flawed training data or altering the classification algorithm to accommodate errors. In contrast, this study explores the concept of tolerating faults during testing by restricting the allowable output range of network activations. In support of this approach, we developed a proof demonstrating that, under specific conditions, a modified network can accurately make classifications when its activation values fall within a predetermined interval, even when it is subjected to stuck-at faults. To validate this concept, we tested it using real-world image classification datasets with both hardware simulators and actual flawed hardware. The results show that the approach can successfully make precise classifications with a moderate increase in computational resources. The proposed technique is also comparable to other fault tolerance methods in terms of accuracy when tested using the MNIST dataset with flawed hardware. The code for this research is available at the URL https://github.com/ghassan-k/FaultTolerantCNN. The proposed interval supervision approach can be combined with other resilience methods to enhance the robustness of convolutional neural networks. The study also presents a roadmap for an official security assessment using this technique. The proposed technique can be applied to various deep learning frameworks, but the research primarily focuses on Caffe. The study further explores the connection between activation interval supervision and the spectral radius of matrix representations of neural networks. The proposed technique can be extended to other types of faults and neural network architectures. The research also presents a theoretical analysis of a simple fully connected neural network. The proposed technique offers numerous potential applications in safety-critical computer vision environments with real-world hardware. Multilingual models are increasingly used for natural language processing tasks that involve multiple languages. These models typically treat languages independently until the model is fine-tuned for specific tasks. However, current methods often fail to leverage the shared underlying semantics across languages. We explore multilingual NLP tasks using monolingual data, assuming each language is represented by a separate vector space without any shared semantics. We propose a novel approach, clustering words across languages to ensure that the vector representations respect the cluster structure. This method yields cluster-specific vector spaces that can be combined into a single shared space, assuming that the semantic structures within clusters are language-independent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on XGLUE, a multilingual dataset, and find that combining the proposed method with a pre-trained multilingual model leads to a 10% improvement in average F1-score compared to a strong baseline. Additionally, we observe that our approach performs significantly better on tasks with limited data. We also analyze the proposed method on the multilingual word similarity task and find it outperforms the current state-of-the-art baseline by 5%. Furthermore, we provide a tool for multilingual word clustering on GitHub. We discuss the challenges remaining in the multilingual NLP domain and propose two research questions in the paper. Lastly, we share experimental setup and additional results in the supplementary material. This study presents measurements of the yields of pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at a 5.44 TeV collision energy. Yields are shown for a range of transverse momentum values (0.2-5 GeV for pions and kaons, 0.4-5 GeV for protons, and 0.4-4 GeV for phi mesons) and centralities ranging from the most central (10% most central collisions) to the most peripheral (70% most peripheral collisions). This ratio also varies with centrality in a similar way for pions, kaons, and phi mesons, but differs for protons. These results are generally consistent with calculations using hydrodynamic models to simulate the collisions, but also reveal differences between protons and other particles. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the presence of wildcards in regular expression patterns. Unlike previous approaches, our technique can effectively handle expressions containing wildcard characters when comparing two regular expressions. We demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts, including the analysis of network protocols and efficient string matching. Furthermore, we have implemented the proposed technique in a tool that utilizes the CLISP interpreter to demonstrate the feasibility of this method for real-world use cases. Our method can also be integrated into existing regular expression analysis tools to enhance their capability in handling wildcard characters. The tool source code is available online for public use. Unlike previous research, our technique can handle the challenge of efficiently detecting the absence of a specific pattern within a set of texts when using regular expressions with wildcard characters. This achievement comes as a result of adapting the concept of small step semantics to regular expression analysis. This adaptation enables the introduction of wildcards as part of the basic set of regular expression operators. We have formally proven the soundness and completeness of this approach. The proposed method can be implemented using a set of basic regular expression operators, including the wildcards '?' and '*'. Mobile agents require accurate navigation, and VIO techniques can provide this by combining information from cameras and inertial sensors. However, these systems typically process large amounts of data from the sensors in limited memory-based models. To address this challenge, we present EMA-VIO, a deep learning-based method for tracking the state of a moving agent using both visual and inertial observations. This model leverages external memory to efficiently manage high-dimensional sensor data, minimizing storage requirements and enabling a more effective and flexible representation of input data. Furthermore, EMA-VIO incorporates an orientation-aware observation model to enhance navigation accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EMA-VIO by applying it to real-world datasets, and it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of navigation accuracy while requiring significantly less memory. Code is available at: https://github.com/ShuaiLuoNPU/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can display
nonlinear phenomena in quantum mechanics. We introduce a new idea where a linear
operator is elevated to a higher order to create a nontrivial effect in a quantum
system. In this study, we develop a linear operator with an elevated order that is
analogue to Weyl semimetals and investigate its implications in both infinite and
finite systems. We demonstrate that certain "Fermi arcs" reappear, and our results
also indicate that the nontrivial effect caused by the elevated order vanishes at
the points of mass generation. In addition, we examine the effect of an external
magnetic field and discover that it transforms the elevated order from a "soccer
ball" shape into a "rugby ball" shape. Our findings suggest that overloading the
elevated order could generate a topological phase in both infinite and finite systems. 
Our research indicates that it is feasible to experimentally realize this novel
elevated-order quantum state in moiré materials formed by stacking graphene layers. 
Our calculations also demonstrate that an external electric field can be used to 
tune the elevated order in these moiré materials. In conclusion, this study provides
a theoretical framework for understanding both general and specific elevated-order 
quantum systems. We anticipate that our research will open up theoretical avenues 
for investigating other nonlinear operator analogues of exotic quantum phenomena. 
Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenghuiLeng/SRW.

This paper introduces a novel framework called Federated Selective Integration for Knowledge Fusion, aimed at efficiently sharing and combining knowledge within a network of autonomous entities. The proposed method leverages a costly initial deep learning model to generate a set of representative data points that serve as inputs for a collective decision-making process. This process involves individual entities making local predictions using their unique data, with the aim of producing diverse outcomes that, when combined, yield a single, high-quality result. The approach minimizes data exchange costs and guarantees improved performance compared to traditional deep learning methods, with benefits demonstrated across real-world applications including classification, regression, and clustering. The code for this method is available at https://github.com/linga2002/Federated-Selective-Integration.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing, where accurate fabrication is crucial. To ensure the quality of these devices, it is essential to have non-invasive detection methods that can accurately assess their components. Specifically for quantum flux parameters in Josephson junctions, it is vital to measure the effective area (Cx) with high precision. To this end, a terahertz near-field nanoscopy technique is employed to determine Cx by directly imaging the harmonic components of microwave fields in planar resonators, thereby enabling the collection of precise data on Josephson junctions and microdisk components. Furthermore, this method is found to be capable of accurately calculating Cx with a precision of 10nm^2, outperforming conventional electrical characterization methods. This terahertz near-field nanoscopy technique is versatile and can be applied to assess complex devices, as well as provide insights into fundamental phenomena, such as high harmonic near-field effects in open resonators. Lastly, this research highlights the vast potential of terahertz near-field nanoscopy in combining with other techniques to advance the fabrication of quantum devices. This study has been published in the scientific journal "Nature Communications".

Today, manually labeling documents for specific data fields is both time-consuming and costly due to their visually complex layout. To make document automation feasible, we propose a new method called "LessLabel," which significantly cuts the number of labels required to train high-performing models in two areas. Firstly, in scenarios where data fields have a consistent structure, we show that just labeling document templates is sufficient to achieve accurate field extraction. Secondly, in cases with variable data structures, we demonstrate that modeling just 10% of the data is enough to achieve results comparable to labeling the entire dataset. To support these claims, we developed a comprehensive evaluation using two popular document types: invoices and resumes. Invoices are renowned for their diverse layouts, presenting a challenging testing ground, while resumes, with their more standardized format, serve as a comparison baseline. Our results show that LessLabel outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by a noticeable margin in both areas. Furthermore, the method's cost-effectiveness is further illustrated by creating a model that can extract data from newly encountered documents with little supervision, using just 13 documents as a training set. This model can then be fine-tuned using just 10% of a larger dataset for even better results. Overall, LessLabel opens up exciting possibilities for applying document automation without incurring exorbitant labeling costs. The method's source code is available for public use at https://github.com/InsightResearchComputing/LessLabel.

These protostars are particularly massive, with accumulated material equivalent to 30 solar masses, and are likely 10 to 100 times more massive than most of their surrounding prestellar cores.  Their development is also distinct from less massive protostars, which typically accumulate material from their surrounding environments over extended periods. This research suggests many massive stars form through such star formations, with ongoing studies also revealing similar phenomena among more distant young star formations.
