This research investigates complex systems that consist of interconnected components, represented as a network, using mathematical models called Gaussian random fields. We focus on analyzing a specific aspect of these models – the way the system's behavior is affected by the way its components bend or vary in relation to each other. We aim to understand how this bending influence changes throughout the system and how it behaves at different points within the system. To achieve this, we use advanced mathematical techniques to break down the system's behavior into simpler components and then reassemble them to gain insight into the bending influence and its behavior. Along the way, we develop a set of mathematical tools that can be applied to other similar systems. Finally, we apply our findings to a specific real-world scenario – the analysis of random temperature fluctuations in time and space. This research is relevant to fields such as economics, biology, and medicine, where understanding complex systems and their interactions is crucial. We also introduce a new statistical measure called the "average bending intensity" that provides a concise summary of the system's behavior. This measure is particularly useful for comparing the complexity of different systems. We demonstrate this by analyzing a simple random system and a more intricate system represented by a network of genetic interactions in yeast. This work is also related to a broader area of research known as "machine learning with Gaussian fields." We believe that our results can be applied to other similar systems and provide a foundation for future research in fields such as statistics, computer science, and biology. One of the most promising techniques for magnetometry, with the ability to achieve extremely low sensitivity limits, is based on atomic interferometry. This method measures the phase shift of an interferometer, caused by the interaction between matter and light, with great precision. However, calculating the phase shift requires knowledge of the precise trajectory followed by atoms as they move through an optical lattice, making it a computationally complex task. Normally, this issue is overcome by conducting experiments under local magnetic fields where the gradient is close to zero, which simplifies the phase shift calculation to be directly proportional to the mass of the atoms. This proportionality makes the measurement extremely sensitive to changes in local magnetic field components, including those that are parallel to the motion of the atoms. This principle was put into practice by using rubidium-87 atomic interferometry to measure the small magnetic fields generated around a nickel nitroprusside complex, as well as to demonstrate the capability to detect very slight alterations in these fields. The outcome not only exceeded the capabilities of over hundred times more expensive magnetic resonance techniques but also reached the level of sensitivity of optical lattice experiments, achieving a record for the smallest measurement of local magnetic field components with atomic interferometry. Furthermore, this work highlighted the advantages of combining atomic interferometry with chemical and biological experiments to detect subtle interactions, in addition to demonstrating the suitability of this technique for analyzing complex molecular magnetic fields and the fields around biological samples. The current setup also allows for the detection of mass changes down to the microgram level, with potential applications in biology and chemistry. The technique is relatively simple to implement, with just a need for a superconducting material to create a Meissner effect, and it offers a wide range of accessible frequency components, including components that are parallel to the motion of the atoms. The achievement of this technique is further reflected in the extremely precise measurement of the mass of a single nickel atom, with implications for the development of precision instruments for chemical and biological analysis. The simplicity of this setup along with the depth of its scientific insights make it suitable for display in a museum. The achievement of this technique also opens up the possibility of using atomic interferometry to detect changes in local magnetic field components caused by dark matter, in addition to the possibility of using it to detect the mass of biological molecules and the mass of individual atoms. This research explores a specific class of mixture models where the components are constructed from subspaces within a high-dimensional data set. We demonstrate that such models can be effectively analyzed using geometric probability, specifically through the theory of random convex bodies. This approach enables us to derive statistical learning results from the geometric properties of the data, and to apply them to synthetic data sets. Furthermore, we connect our findings to general theoretical frameworks, specifically to advances in high-dimensional statistics and to a particular model where the components are sparse, which can be viewed as a geometric interpretation of the Lasso algorithm. Lastly, we discuss potential applications to real-world data analysis problems.

We present DynaSOAr, a high-performance memory allocator tailored for OpenCL on NVIDIA GPUs. This allocator leverages concurrent access to internal pointers within the memory blocks, enabling efficient and lock-free management of memory through "first-come, first-served" execution. Additionally, DynaSOAr employs a stack-based allocation strategy, specifically optimized for deep recursion techniques commonly found in certain physics simulations that utilize object-oriented programming. Compared to other memory allocators and lock-free approaches, DynaSOAr's performance stands out in various benchmarks, with gains of up to 2.5 times in open-source OpenCL applications. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's compact size makes it an attractive choice for memory-constrained GPU applications, with a notable reduction of 128 bytes per thread compared to the existing OpenCL stack allocator. Source code for DynaSOAr is available under the permissive BSD license.

A theoretical framework for the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states that forms between a quasiparticle and a localized magnetic impurity on a superconducting surface has been developed. This model, supported by an initial principles method, accurately describes local magnetic moments's influence on the YSR states. It was found that the YSR states's behavior in a chain of dimers is governed by both the inter- and the intra-dimer interactions. This theoretical analysis was applied to both an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on a Nb(110) surface, and it was discovered that YSR states's binding energies in a chain of dimers exhibit both inter- and intra-dimer interactions, which could be either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic. This theory was compared to experimental data obtained using a low-temperature scanning tunneling microscope, and it was found that it accurately describes the behavior of YSR states in both cases. This theoretical analysis also highlights the importance of considering both the inter- and the intra-dimer interactions in a chain of YSR states's binding energies in order to accurately describe their behavior in both cases. This finding provides further evidence for the magnetic dipole-dipole interaction's role in determining the YSR states's behavior in a chain of dimers. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Ultimately, the team recommends observing TOI-712 with spectroscopic instruments to uncover the planets' atmospheric properties and study the system's astronomical phenomena in detail. Recently, a class of non-abelian gauge theories known as scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in (1+1) dimensions have been successfully simulated using qudits with various trimerizations. These simulations can either use closed systems to produce periodic signals or closed systems to generate signal fragments. Due to the complexity of the spectrum in closed systems, some "hidden" resonances with large signal amplitudes can go undetected unless specific careful searches are conducted. This study examined the simulation of sQED using qudits in closed systems with trimerizations other than the standard trichromatism. A general method for simulating this model was developed, and it was discovered that trichromatism can significantly influence the amplitude of certain resonances, making some qudits much more effective at simulating sQED. In fact, one qudit, the tritetrachromatism, was found to possess a resonance with an exceptionally large amplitude, surpassing the amplitude of the corresponding resonance in the standard trichromatism qudit by an incredible 250 times after adjusting for detuning. In addition, it was discovered that trichromatism can also influence the system's dynamics by displacing the resonances' frequency and altering their widths. As a result, there are many untapped possibilities for improving qudit simulations simply by switching to a different trichromatism, and researchers are now advised to provide detailed information about their trichromatism when sharing simulation data. Moreover, qudits with dynamic trichromatism, which can change over time, have been discovered and proven to be a valuable tool for simultaneously avoiding resonances while increasing the signal amplitude. In conclusion, this study has unlocked several valuable insights that are relevant to a broad range of simulations, including but not limited to sQED. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, transparent target. We find that the positron population becomes polarized by more than tenfold due to the interaction of the positrons with the intense laser field as it enters the positrons' vicinity. Furthermore, we identify parameters for which the positrons exhibit double polarization, with an order of magnitude increase in the number of polarized positrons compared to non-polarized counterparts. We also determine the influence of the target thickness and laser properties on the generated polarized positrons. This research develops a temperature detection system that operates across a wide range of voltages from 0.6V to 1.8V and is suitable for integrating into memory chips. The proposed design leverages threshold voltage variations due to oxide trap formation as a means of temperature measurement, offering a precise and reliable method with a small area requirement. By utilizing multiple trip points defined by different supply voltages, the design ensures accurate temperature readings across a broad range of thresholds and trap distributions. Furthermore, using simulation results, we validated our proposed concept and tested it under real-world conditions, comparing its performance to experimental data obtained from a specific 90nm CMOS technology. The proposed design was found to match the experimental data closely, with some minor discrepancies attributed to difficulties in modeling trap distributions. The temperature detection system was found to provide a precise reading within a $\pm$1.4{\deg}C error margin and required only a minimal amount of additional circuitry, just 1.06nJ per conversion, to function. Moreover, the design offered a suitable resolution of 0.24{\deg}C and was compatible with low voltage and low power design requirements for integrated memory applications. The proposed temperature detection system was also capable of monitoring temperatures across a wide range of values, from 0{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C, and the design's effectiveness was further demonstrated through practical implementation on a test chip using the mentioned 90nm CMOS technology. Furthermore, we explore the integration of geometric frameworks in relation to the integration of Lie groupoids. A recent survey of far-infrared bright cores in the Dragon infrared dark nebula reveals the presence of massive protostar and star-forming cores.  Analyzing these cores, we find that they are concentrated in the nebula's center and exhibit similar velocities to the surrounding gas and dust.  By combining kinematic and thermodynamic data, we determine that these cores possess sufficient mass and angular momentum to form a massive stellar core with $M_{\rm core} \approx 40 M_{\sun}$, and are thus likely precursors to massive star formation.  Furthermore, the absence of outflows or massive dense cores suggests that these cores are immature, and the nebula's dynamics are influenced by the gravitational pull of a massive, unseen central object.  Using simple modeling, we propose that the nebula is entangled with the Mon R2 HII region through a filament that spans 20 pc, and that this entanglement prevented it from collapsing into a massive star.  Instead, it gave rise to the young T Tauri stars and brown dwarfs found in its center.  We suggest that this outcome is likely for many similar infrared dark nebulae, and that many low-mass T Tauri stars and brown dwarfs may have similar parent nebulae.  Future surveys of the ISM with high angular resolution and molecular line observations will be capable of detecting similar cores and entangled filaments, and can shed more light on the formation and disintegration of massive stellar cores.  Additionally, the study of one such core in the Taurus complex is presented as an appendix.  The core, named TMC-D, has a mass similar to the solar mass, and is composed of a slowly rotating sun-like star and a slowly rotating brown dwarf.  TMC-D is comparable to well-known T Tauri associations, but unlike them, it does not have any outflows or gas associated with it, and instead, it is similar to the subpopulation of T Tauri stars found in the Carina Nebula.  The two components of TMC-D are likely separated by a distance of 3.7 pc, and are moving in opposite directions at speeds of up to 0.8 km/s.  The study suggests that TMC-D may have originated from the collapse of a massive prestellar core, and that its disintegration led to the formation of the sun and the brown dwarf. The interaction between a moving object and a complex surface is influenced by the object's velocity, surface properties, and the properties of the surrounding fluid. When an object moves through a fluid-filled channel, especially one with a rough texture, its movement can be opposed by an equivalent force. This force is known as drag and can vary significantly based on the velocity of the object and the characteristics of the channel. In the course of conducting experiments with a glass rod moving through films of different surfactants, we observed an unusual increase in the force opposing the motion when a particular texture was present. This increase in opposing force was found to change depending on the velocity of the rod and was greater in fluids with higher viscosity. In addition, when the surfactant was altered, changes occurred in the texture of the fluid and the opposing force also changed as a result. These findings can be applied to similar real-world situations like the movement of a leg through a muddy pond. In such scenarios, the texture of the mud can create a force opposing the movement that varies based on the velocity of the movement and the composition of the mud. In such situations, the movement of an object through a fluid-filled channel is opposed by an equivalent force that can create nonlinear patterns in the texture of the fluid. The number of skin cancer cases is rising worldwide, necessitating early and accurate diagnosis to increase treatment effectiveness.  In this research, we develop a 3D convolutional neural network named SCCNet to automatically identify skin carcinomas from medical images.  SCCNet's design enables it to determine both carcinomas and outliers in images by outputting two probability maps.  We test the network using publicly available data and compare its performance to that of existing competing methods.  Furthermore, we create and share a new dataset consisting of 3D dermoscopy images of melanoma lesions, contributing to the advancement of research in this area.  Our findings demonstrate that SCCNet delivers superior performance in both classification and outlier detection tasks.  We also explore the relationship between outlier areas and carcinomas, finding that in dermoscopy images, outliers are frequently associated with malignant melanoma.  As a result, we propose using dermoscopy images of melanoma lesions for training models.  This research received a grant from the King Saud University, Research Group Project Number RPDP1-004.  We share the trained model and dermoscopy images of melanoma lesions with the research community via a public repository.  This model achieves an accuracy of 92.3% in detecting carcinomas and 88.3% in identifying dermoscopy images of melanoma lesions.  However, this model has limitations, primarily related to image quality and the small sample size used in its development.  We suggest several modifications to improve the model, including using transfer learning, combining features with deep learning, and using longer range dependencies.  We provide free access to the dermoscopy images of melanoma lesions via a public repository, inviting other researchers to contribute additional data and improve the model further.  This model has the potential to be adapted for clinical use after undergoing proper validation in a controlled clinical setting. The significant discrepancy between high-performance computing and distributed systems has long been acknowledged and poses a substantial barrier for various computing domains. A parallel exists between the varying realms of numerical linear solvers and partial differential equation solvers, and researchers have also noted the gap between these areas. In response to this challenge, researchers are advocating for the development of high-performance algorithms tailored for complex systems of multiple variables. In contrast, the majority of research focuses on smaller systems with fewer variables. To bridge the mentioned disparity, a new category of algorithms, known as scalable linear solvers, has been proposed. These solvers leverage the availability of massive computing resources to achieve high-speed performance in large-scale linear systems of equations. A key feature of these solvers is that they can handle sparse matrix representations, which are inherently efficient. The development of these solvers is also motivated by the advancement of unstructured grid methods, particularly finite element techniques. The implementation of these solvers is discussed in the context of the Transputer-based grid computing system, and their performance is compared to that of a state-of-the-art numerical solver on a complex PDE problem arising in the study of turbulent fluids. The research also explores various optimization techniques for these solvers on this particular grid platform. The proposed algorithms can be applied to a wide range of linear solving problems involving sparse matrices and have been made available as part of the public domain FINELM numerical solver package. The package supports multiple processing elements and provides high-performance performance on complex systems of equations. This work introduces a novel method, SFSSX, for analyzing multivariate functions that contain singularities across different dimensional spaces. Unlike its predecessor, the singular spectrum test, SFSSX can handle non-integer dimensional spaces and combines the advantages of both wavelet thresholding and multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis. The method's performance is assessed through Monte Carlo simulations, and its applicability is demonstrated using synthetic data with multiple variables and real-world data from the field of geophysics. The framework for SFSSX is then expanded to create the multivariate functional multi-resolution singular spectrum test, SFMMRX, which enables the identification and extraction of signals with non-isotropic properties from multivariate functional data. The results obtained from both simulations and real-data applications highlight the effectiveness and flexibility of SFSSX and SFMMRX in a broad range of scenarios. The code associated with this study is made available online to facilitate further development and adaptation of the methods presented. This study investigates the long-term behavior of a stochastic process known as local time divided by its mean, which is extracted from one-dimensional random walks. We establish that this process converges asymptotically as time approaches infinity with a specific probability distribution as its underlying parameter varies. Notably, when the random walk's displacement follows a power-law distribution with specific exponents, we find that this process converges to either a delta function or a continuous probability distribution, depending on these exponents. Additionally, we compare our findings with results from existing research to demonstrate that the asymptotic distribution we identify is robust and exhibits only a minor discrepancy when the walk's displacement distribution deviates slightly from a normal distribution. Moreover, we provide a numerical technique for calculating the asymptotic distribution and examine its properties in detail. Lastly, the study also incorporates an explicit expression for the asymptotic distribution when the random walk's displacement undergoes a second-order stationary process, which provides further insights and serves as a starting point for future analysis. The research is further illustrated with an example involving sinusoidal random walks. The results we derived are intended to contribute to the broader field of stochastic processes and may also have implications for the asymptotic behavior of other processes with similar characteristics. The IShTAR plasma generator at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics has been analyzed to understand its operation in helicon mode. A review of existing research on similar plasma sources, particularly the helicon source, is conducted to gain insight into its physics. A study on the IShTAR plasma source reveals that it operates in a transitional regime between helicon and E-edge plasma modes. To validate the findings, a comparison is drawn between the measured and calculated values of plasma parameters in both helicon and E-edge modes. The results indicate that the plasma density in helicon mode is overestimated by a factor of ten when calculated without considering the occurrence of the E-edge mode. Furthermore, it is found that the plasma density in helicon mode is independent of the magnetic field strength but reliant on the length of the magnetic field extension. In E-edge mode, the plasma density is found to increase with the magnetic field strength and field extension length. In helicon mode, the ratio of the plasma density to the electron temperature also remains constant across different plasma source configurations. In E-edge mode, this ratio fluctuates. In helicon mode, the plasma electron temperature is found to be independent of the distance from the plasma source, whereas in E-edge mode, the electron temperature decreases with distance. In helicon mode, the ratio of the plasma density to the electron temperature is comparable to that observed in other helicon sources. In E-edge mode, this ratio is lower than in helicon mode. In helicon mode, the plasma sheath length is found to be independent of the distance from the plasma source, and the plasma density at the plasma source is found to be higher than in E-edge mode. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effective deployment of such technology in clinical settings is hindered by difficulties in gathering large datasets for training and testing. To address this challenge, a research team created an automated dataset generator utilizing advanced image processing techniques. Nevertheless, even with this tool, researchers face another obstacle in validating predicted results, as it is equally difficult to gather large quantities of manually annotated nucleus segments for evaluation purposes. To tackle this issue, a novel method called W-Net was developed, which combines a nucleus segmentation module with a nucleus removal module to effectively leverage intrinsic relationships between images and their processed variants. As a result, this network is capable of generating high-quality evaluation datasets for free. To validate the effectiveness of W-Net, researchers tested it using two different datasets, with the resulting scores indicating that it ranks among the top performing nucleus segmentation algorithms across various metrics. Furthermore, to demonstrate the versatility of W-Net, researchers also used processed variants of cells to train a cancer diagnosis classifier using a minimal amount of dataset, which led to a notable improvement in classification accuracy. Ultimately, this research paves the way for secure deployment of nucleus segmentation technology in clinical settings by providing a reliable method for generating high-quality annotation datasets for free. This approach is particularly suitable for cancer diagnosis, where precise annotation requires an inordinate amount of time and effort. Elastography, an imaging technique that utilizes tissue displacement under external forces to differentiate soft tissues based on their mechanical properties, has the potential to revolutionize clinical diagnostics. In large-scale encounters between a pursuer and multiple evaders, the pursuer often relies on the environment and local interactions with the evaders to guide it towards a successful capture. We have developed a hierarchical model to explore the strategic decisions made by a pursuer in a stochastic pursuit-evasion game. This hierarchical framework divides the decision process into two levels: a high-level section that focuses on overall progress towards the goal, and a lower-level section that handles local movements. Through extensive simulations, we observed how the pursuer's hierarchical decisions affected its ability to capture evaders in varying environments. Furthermore, we found that the hierarchical structure enables the pursuer to adapt to dynamic environments by hierarchically updating its probability distribution. Lastly, in a scenario with multiple pursuers, we observed how the hierarchical structure affects cooperation and spatial division among the pursuers. Together, these findings provide a deeper understanding of the hierarchical decision-making processes involved in pursuit-evasion games. In complex situations with multiple related tasks, using models in multi-task reinforcement learning can lead to significant improvements, but underlying structural relationships among tasks can also cause issues. Specifically, when tasks share features, they can compete and exhibit destructive interference, resulting in slow learning and poor performance. To address this problem, we develop a general method using modular systems to separate feature spaces among tasks, thereby preventing destructive interference and allowing for better-than-expect performance. Furthermore, this method is adaptable to changing environments and can handle changes in task relationships. To evaluate our method, we created the Competing Circuits experiment, which simulates co- existing neural circuits competing for shared resources, and found it to be effective in both static and dynamically changing scenarios. Lastly, we applied this method to a real-world problem, with promising results. All code used in this study is available online.

We create a formal system whose theories mirror the lifestyles of its four creators. This system is designed to ascertain how logicians live in a world where formal systems govern truth-telling. We then examine the world defined by this system for its inherent consistency, discovering that it isn't fundamentally consistent. In response, we modify the system to make its world more consistent, albeit at the cost of making truth a relative concept. Ultimately, we show that even with this adjustment, the system cannot be considered fundamentally reliable in defining what is true. This finding leads us to contemplate the implications for the practice of logic-based world-building. Additionally, we offer a concise proof of a previously known but formerly unpublished result regarding the system's reliability. Lastly, we conclude by examining the system's connection to a specific problem known as the "Godel world problem." This problem, first posed by Godel, asks if it's possible to create a formal system that accurately represents a world where arithmetic facts are universally known. We demonstrate that even with the system we've developed, it's impossible to create such a system for a specific, narrowly defined "Godel world." This system has the added benefit of allowing us to explore the concept of a world where arithmetic facts aren't universally known. This world is analogous to another world described by Tarski in his famous paper "The Concept of Truth in Formalized Languages." mathematical framework, known as the posterior data model, which links the
process of image formation to the corresponding forward model. We can derive the
likelihood function of the data distribution using this model, thereby making it
possible to employ Bayesian methods for image restoration. However, one major
obstacle in this approach is the difficulty in computing the posterior
distribution of the data, a problem we attempt to solve by proposing a novel

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through modified dilated convolution layers that account for periodic information, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in generating speech with specific frequencies. To achieve this, QPNet employs a novel Transposed Overlap And Add (TOAA) algorithm that combines the results of autoregressive dilated convolution layers from the current and previous time frames, allowing the model to leverage contextual information for better speech synthesis. Furthermore, we introduce a method to train the model using a combination of mean squared error and multi-scale spectrogram reconstruction loss, resulting in a more robust and generalizable model. Experimental evaluations reveal that QPNet outperforms WN and other speech generative models in terms of naturalness, and its ability to produce high-fidelity speech at specific frequencies is unparalleled. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential of QPNet to generate polyphonic speech by incorporating multiple frequency components, and the model's efficiency, with a parameter count comparable to WN. The code for this research is available open-source on GitHub.

The bicategorical shadow functor associates bicategories to a particular class of functors that involve rearranging objects for the purpose of studying bicategorical invariants. When the base bicategory is symmetric, this functor can be viewed as constructing symmetric bicategories from certain types of functors. A key observation is that these bicategorical shadows come equipped with a structure consisting of natural transformations, essentially capturing the essence of the functors that gave rise to them. A further discovery reveals that the shadow functor preserves bicategorical localizations, provided they are obtained using certain defining properties.
